task: Each item gives a public decision (source) and a record. Report whether the record drops dates or attributed speakers that the source gives, and which.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Purchasing Agent at the Agency’s VA Medical Center in Decatur, Georgia. On August 12, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the basis of disability (anxiety; depression) when: 1. On June 2 and 3, 2020, Complainant was questioned about the leave she had taken under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and 2. On June 2, 3, and 24, 2020, Complainant was charged Absent Without Leave (AWOL). 2 Complainant stated that she has major depression and anxiety. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 66. She asserted that on June 3, 2020, her Supervisor questioned her about her FMLA leave which she asserted was “targeting” her due to her disability by marking her AWOL even though she was on FMLA leave. See ROI at 68. She acknowledged that after she told them about her FMLA leave, the Chief told her that the AWOL would be removed. See ROI at 69. The Supervisory Purchasing Agent (Supervisor) stated that the Chief of Prosthetics had him reach out to Complainant to clarify the situation with Complainant’s leave because HR had only provided the FMLA paperwork for January to February 2020 when it was requested. See ROI at 144-45. He asserted that once Complainant had verified that she had approved FMLA leave, her AWOL was removed. See ROI at 147. The Assistant Chief of Prosthetics (Assistant Chief) confirmed that Complainant was never officially marked AWOL and once her FMLA was verified, he instructed the timekeeper to enter in Complainant’s time as FMLA as required. See ROI at 124-25. Complainant’s time sheet records confirm that Complainant was not actually marked AWOL on the dates at issue. See ROI at 157. The Agency’s acceptance letter erroneously listed only June 24, 2020 as the date on which Complainant alleged she was charged AWOL but the investigation was later clarified at Complainant’s request to include June 2 and 3, 2020. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 31-36. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. On May 16, 2022, the Agency filed a motion for a decision without a hearing to which Complainant did not respond. The AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s motion and issued a decision without a hearing on June 16, 2022. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Claims Technical Expert (CTE), GS-0105-12, at the Agency’s Great Lakes Program Service Center in Chicago, Illinois. Complainant received a reprimand on July 20, 2021, for conduct unbecoming a federal employee. The reprimand cited two specifications: on June 16, 2021, Complainant refused to provide a status update on assigned cases, raised her voice, and continued to refuse during a subsequent meeting; and on June 23, 2021, she refused assistance with a mainframe password issue, leading to a two-hour work delay. Complainant’s first-line supervisor, Module Manager (S1), asserted that requesting status updates and assisting with password issues were common management practices. Complainant also claimed workplace harassment, alleging that S1 assigned duties preventing her from completing primary CTE tasks and treated her differently from other CTEs. She complained of accusatory, condescending, and rude communication. Complainant alleged that the reprimand itself constituted harassment, tarnishing her character, and that the issuance of a 3. Performance Assessment Communications Systems (PACS) rating for Fiscal Year 2021, lower than a prior 4. PAC rating in Fiscal Year 2019, was harassment. Complainant reported these concerns to the union and management. S1 denied the allegations explaining that work assignments aligned with the week's plan and that management routinely assisted employees with password issues. S1 denied claims of harassment in assigning duties and asserted that the reprimand and rating were issued in line with standard practices. On November 11, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment on the bases of race (African-American), sex (female), color (Black), age (63), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. On July 20, 2021, she received a reprimand; and 2. Beginning June 23, 2021 and present, with regard to work assignments, assignment of duties, condescending comments, spoken to in a loud voice, lowered PACS, reprimand, and questioning time to work on inquiries. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In the decision, the Agency determined that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. The Agency dismissed an additional allegation as untimely raised with an EEO Counselor. Complainant raised no challenges regarding this matter on appeal and the Commission can find no basis to disturb the Agency’s dismissal decision. The Commission will, however, consider the claim as background evidence in support of Complainant’s hostile work environment claim.

On April 22, 2021, she received derogatory comments from the Commander in a “Reply All” email such as “I hope it is not your intention to allow the contractor to not complete this work. That is unacceptable.” c. When on or about April 26, 2021, she received an email reply from the Commander which told her he never had to have a conversation with someone of her rank or responsibility and asks if it alarms her since it was concerning to him; d. When on July 6, 2021, the Manager issued her a Letter of Expectations based on email feedback from the Commander. 2 Complainant was assigned to work as the Project Manager (PM) for the Maintenance Team of the USS Cole in December 2020, a position which entailed being responsible for expediting product completion deadlines and serving the customer, i.e., the USS Cole and its Commander, and ship forces. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 176; 613-21. The Commander stated that it was the usual practice for the PM to hold production meetings on the ship each day with the USS Cole’s leadership and respective contractors, which allowed for leaders to proactively socialize maintenance problems and solutions. See ROI at 458. He stated that the Commanding Officer and the PM were expected to work together to unite the maintenance team and ship’s force to complete the maintenance package on time. See ROI at 458. He stated that when Complainant started as the PM, he was upfront about the daily meeting requirement and was frank about the challenges that he and the previous PM had faced. See ROI at 459. He explained that the emails he sent her were to provide feedback about the status of the work being untimely and done with poor workmanship. See ROI at 460. He further explained that in his opinion, Complainant’s referring to any communication issues that led to the job being late or incomplete was due to Complainant’s own refusal to hold daily meetings. See ROI at 460. He stated that people at their level and pay grade were expected to execute at the highest levels and not allow excuses to get in the way of what is right for the ship, which always takes precedence. See ROI at 462. Complainant responded to that email by referring to her protected classes, stating “Please understand that I am a mid-level GS-13 Civil Service Employee with protected status under four categories: black, female, over 40 and disabled.” See ROI at 463. The Manager stated that he issued the Letter of Expectations after this email because he found it to be unprofessional and inappropriate for Complainant to bring up her protected classes because it was not germane to the conversation. See ROI at 435. He further explained that the Letter of Expectations was not disciplinary or a negative action. See ROI at 436. The Agency dismissed a claim that between June 2020 and November 2020, the commander of the USS Ramage yelled at her, stood in the way of timely project completion, and sent her command derogatory comments regarding her performance pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(2) for untimely counselor contact. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 137-39. Complainant stated that she felt the Commander’s emails to be demeaning because he was correcting her about something when he is a peer and not a supervisor. See ROI at 180. She asserted that she believed the Commander’s treatment of her and her supervisor’s lack of response to her allegation of harassment had to do with her protected classes because “[t]hey do not do this to people who are not a marginalized group in [her] experience.” See ROI at 182. Complainant acknowledged, however, that the only way in which she tried to make her supervisors aware of the alleged harassment was by adding her first-line supervisor (Supervisor) to the email chain with the Commander. See ROI at 181. Both the Coordinator and the Manager stated that to their knowledge, Complainant never actually mentioned that she believed she was being subjected to harassment to anyone in management. See ROI at 421; 434. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s April 1, 2022, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on April 27, 2022. The AJ found that Complainant could not establish a prima facie case with respect to the Letter of Expectations and even if she could, there was no evidence to indicate it was due to discriminatory animus. The AJ further found that all of the alleged incidents of harassment taken together were not sufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute an unlawful hostile work environment. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed but did not make any specific arguments on appeal. In response, the Agency contends that the AJ correctly found that there was no evidence beyond Complainant’s bare assertions to indicate any discriminatory animus.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Budget Analyst at the Agency’s Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE) Office in Washington, D.C. In the Agency’s July 22, 2021, acceptance of Complainant’s May 14, 2021, amendment request, the Agency noted that reprisal only applied to claim 2 as Complainant alleged that her protected EEO activity was the instant complaint. 1. on or around February 1, 2021, Complainant was informed by email that the Department’s tentative job offer to Complainant for the position of Budget Director, EERE, had been rescinded; and 2. on May 14, 2021, Complainant was not selected for the position of Budget Director. Complainant worked in the Department’s Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE) as a Budget Analyst, in Washington, D.C., from September 10, 2018, until March 10, 2021. Report of Investigation, Part 1 (ROI1) at 279. From approximately October 2019 until March 10, 2021, Complainant also served as the Acting Budget Director. ROI1 at 312. On December 30, 2020, Complainant received a tentative job offer for the position of Budget Director, EERE Office. ROI1 at 153. On January 20, 2021, the Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary (Principal), began her position as the new Principal and Acting Assistant Secretary for EERE. Once in position, the Principal stated that she studied position descriptions for various key positions to ensure that the organization was structured appropriately. ROI1 at 391. She found that many position descriptions did not accurately reflect what was needed. For the Budget Director position in particular, the Principal noted that the position was “watered down” and did not require specialized budget expertise. Additionally, her review also led to the Federal Energy Management Program Director position being reclassified. SROI at 60. On February 1, 2021, Complainant was informed by email that the Agency’s tentative job offer to Complainant for the position of Budget Director had been rescinded. ROI1 at 185. The letter informed Complainant, in part, the following: Based on expansive platform changes which will heavily impact EERE programs, the Budget Director role in EERE must be updated to reflect the changed priorities of the Administration and the Department, as well as the specialized budget formulation and execution expertise and broader responsibilities of the position to address the anticipated increases in appropriations for EERE programs. The Director stated that based on responses to the standard six questions asked of each candidate, Complainant’s score was lower than the three candidates selected as Best Qualified. SROI at 71. The Deputy Assistant stated that she made her decision based on the recommendation of the interview panel. SROI at 143-147. items.source: During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Vocational Rehabilitation Specialist at the Agency’s Behavioral Service Line, Gulf Coast Health Care facility in Biloxi, Mississippi. Compensated Work Therapy Program Manager (Manager) was her first-level supervisor. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 85, 119. 1. On October 15, 2019, Manager, issued Complainant a sick leave certification letter; 2. On November 13, 2019, Manager issued Complainant a Letter of Admonishment; and 3. On November 20, 2019, Manager rated Complainant lower than deserved on her annual performance evaluation. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case determined sua sponte that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and over Complainant's objections, issued a decision without a hearing on March 4, 2022. The AJ found that the Agency provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions for each claim. In claim 1, the AJ noted that Manager issued Complainant a sick leave certification at the recommendation of Labor and Employee Relations. Complainant used 107 hours of sick leave between April 15 and October 10, 2019. ROI at 126. The sick leave had two concerning patterns. When Manager assigned Complainant a patient, Complainant would enter sick leave into the leave system, send Manager an email, and then go home. The second pattern was one in which Complainant would take sick leave on days immediately surrounding days when she was scheduled to be off work. ROI at 127. As to claim 2, Manager issued Complainant a proposed admonishment on October 22, 2019, for conduct and behavior issues. ROI at 30. There were six specifications enumerated on the proposed admonishment. Two of these specifications involved telling Manager not to come to scheduled meetings and four were concerning Complainant’s unwillingness to respond to Manager’s instructions. Id. After the proper procedure was followed, Manager upheld the admonishment on November 13, 2019. ROI at 276. Regarding claim 3, Manager asserted that he took the concerns outlined in the proposed admonishment into account with Complainant’s performance review. He found that Complainant did her job but did not perform beyond that which was expected. As such, he rated Complainant “fully successful” for her performance review. ROI at 143-149. The AJ found that Complainant was unable to provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate pretext. As such, Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant raised generalized concerns regarding the lack of discovery due to the issuance of summary judgment.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Contract Surveillance Representative, GS-9, at the Agency’s Armed Forces Retirement Home, Washington Campus, in Washington, D.C. Complaint #1: [number removed] On April 5, 2021, Complainant filed Complaint #1 alleging discrimination based on race (African American), color (other than white), sex (female), and in reprisal (for the exercise of Title VII rights and for seeking union protection and reporting behavior and contract performance issues), when: 1. On an unspecified date, she was denied a promotion. 2. On unspecified dates, she was excluded from staff activities. 3. From July 2019 to January 2020, Contract Project Manager, Armed Forces Retirement Home, yelled at her while on site visits, and made comments, such as, “I’m sick of [Complainant],” “[Complainant] gets on my nerves,” and “Watch out for [Complainant].” 4. On January 14, 2020, her supervisor (S1), Chief, Resident Services, GS-14, instructed her to send emails upon her arrival and departure from work. 5. On January 17, 2020, S1 removed her as the Contracting Surveillance Representative for Global Connections to Employment duties. 6. On January 17, 2020, September 30, 2019, and June 2, 2019, S1 issued her Letters of Counseling. 7. In March and July 2020, S1 denied her request for telework and hazard pay. 8. In July 2020, S1 issued her a rating of 1 (Unsatisfactory) for Fiscal Year 2020 after revising her Strategic Goal performance element without notice or her participating in her performance plans. 9. On December 15, 2020, S1 threatened to demote her, removed her Contract Officer Representative duties, and “put [her] in a corner” of the office. 10. On January 11, 2021, S1 placed her on an Opportunity to Improve. 11. On January 21, 2021, she was made aware Human Resources did not process her union dues for six months and refused to provide the union’s correct contact information. 12. In February 2021, Senior Financial Analyst, Armed Forces Retirement Home, sent emails and text messages with rude slurs, sexual graphics, and asking the question, “How’s life on the plantation.” 13. On March 24, 2021, Human Resources Specialist denied her request for tuition reimbursement stating the Agency does not have a tuition reimbursement program. On June 10, 2021, the Agency accepted claims 10 and 13 as discrete acts and accepted claims 4 – 10 and 13 as part of the hostile work environment claim. The Agency dismissed claims 1 and 2, for failure to provide clarifying information and dismissed claims 3, 11, and 12 for failure to state a claim, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.107(a)(7) and .107(a)(1), respectively. The Agency dismissed the discrete portion of claims 4 – 8 due to untimely EEO Counselor contact pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(2) but accepted those as part of the hostile work environment claim. The Agency also dismissed Complainant’s alleged basis of reprisal because her filing a complaint against Human Resources office for not posting union representatives contact information did not constitute protected activity within the meaning of the EEO regulations. The Agency further stated that Complainant did not allege that she addressed a discriminatory issue in that complaint against Human Resources office. The Agency investigated the accepted claims from July 22 to September 1, 2021. The Agency indicated that on September 15, 2021, it provided, via certified mail, Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). The Agency stated that Complainant reported she did not receive the mail and thus, on October 14, 2021, it reissued a copy of the report of investigation along with her right to hearing, via Agency’s Secure Access File Exchange filesharing electronic system, to Complainant. Complaint #2: [number removed] On July 9, 2021, Complainant filed Complaint #2 alleging discrimination based on race (African American), disability, sex (female), and in reprisal for prior EEO activity when: 14. On June 7, 2021, she was denied Family and Medical Leave Act leave for her May 2021 surgery. 15. On an unknown date, she was denied her reasonable accommodation request for telework and a handicap parking space. On July 30, 2021, the Agency dismissed claim 15 for raising a matter that had not been brought to the attention of an EEO Counselor, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2). The Agency investigated claim 14 from August 30 through September 28, 2021. The Agency indicated that on October 14, 2021, the Agency, via its Secure Access File Exchange filesharing electronic system, provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation, including a notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. The Agency stated that it reissued the report of investigation on October 27, 2021, and again on November 10, 2021, because Complainant did not retrieve the original notices. On January 26, 2022, the Agency, consolidated the complaints and issued a final Agency decision finding no discrimination as alleged. The Agency stated that Complainant failed to make an election to request a hearing by the deadline, i.e., by November 13, 2021 (30-days after October 14, 2021) for Complaint #1, and by December 10, 2021 (30-days after November 10, 2021) for Complaint #2. On March 18, 2022, Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision indicating that the Agency’s final decision was “wrong,” and there was an error in the Agency’s processing of her claims. In response to Complainant’s appeal, the Agency indicated that Complainant’s appeal should be denied as untimely. Specifically, the Agency stated that Complainant received the final Agency decision on January 26, 2022, but she did not file an appeal until March 18, 2022, which was beyond the 30-day time limit. In the alternative, stated the Agency, the Commission should affirm its final decision finding no discrimination. The record reveals that on October 6, 2021, Complainant, via EEOC Public Portal, requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ for both complaints and uploaded a copy of a Request for a Hearing Form, dated September 30, 2021, for Complaint #1, which was docketed under Hearing No. 570- 2022-00017X; and a copy of a Request for a Hearing Form, dated October 1, 2021, for Complaint #2, which was docketed under Hearing No. 570-2022-00018X. The record indicates that on January 24, 2022, the AJ issued a Notice of Intent to Sanction for each complaint because the Agency failed to submit the complaint file and/or the report of investigation. On March 24, 2022, the Agency filed a separate response to each Notice of Intent to Sanction, indicating that sanctions against the Agency were not warranted because it was not served with a notice that Complainant filed a hearing request, and it was not on notice of any order or other requirement until March 10, 2022. Specifically, the Agency stated that Complainant did not use Request for a Hearing Form that was provided to her when the report of investigation was transmitted to her. In that form, Complainant was informed to choose the Agency, in EEOC Public Portal, as “DoD Office of Secretary/Washington Headquarters Services.” Instead, Complainant used an outdated version of Request for a Hearing Form which did not indicate an option to request a hearing in the EEOC Public Portal and thus no instruction choosing the Agency therein. The Agency stated that Complainant’s hearings were docketed, via EEOC Public Portal, with the Agency as “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” on October 6, 2021. At that time, the Agency EEO Program Director (“EEOP Director”) or the Agency’s EEO office did not have access to “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” via FedSEP and thus, the Agency never received the October 6, 2021, filings. The Agency indicated that on March 10, 2022, the EEOP Director requested and received access to the “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” FedSEP box as a stopgap measure while discussing with individuals at the EEOC (Office of Federal Operations and Washington Field Office) other ways to ensure more effective usage of FedSEP, given the large population, consisting of multiple agencies, serviced by “DoD Office of Secretary/Washington Headquarters Services.” On March 10, 2022, the EEOP Director promptly uploaded a copy of the final Agency decision in FedSEP, and on March 11, 2022, the Agency counsel requested an extension to respond to the AJ’s Notice of Intent to Sanction. The Agency argued that the AJ should dismiss Complainant’s hearing requests because they were not properly filed. The Agency indicated that Complainant did not send a copy of the hearing requests to the Agency’s EEO office as instructed and as such it properly issued a final Agency decision for both complaints. The Agency stated that Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision and the AJ proceeding with a hearing would be inappropriate. Further, the Agency stated that the AJ lacked jurisdiction to hear Complainant’s complaints because Complainant filed her hearing requests prematurely before her receipt of the investigative report and before 180 days had elapsed under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(h). The Agency indicated that regarding Complaint #1, filed on April 5, 2021, Complainant’s hearing request form was dated September 30, 2021, i.e., before she received the reissued investigative report on October 14, 2021, and before 180 days had elapsed from the filing of the complaint. Regarding Complaint #2, filed on July 9, 2021, the Agency stated that Complainant’s hearing request form was dated October 1, 2021, i.e., before she received the investigative report on November 10, 2021, and only 84 days after the filing of a formal complaint. Based on the foregoing, the Agency asked the AJ to withdraw the Notice of Intent to Sanction the Agency and dismiss Complainant’s hearing requests as they were not properly filed and because the AJ lacked jurisdiction. On May 6, 2022, Complainant submitted to the AJ a motion, in part, to consolidate cases, motion for sanctions, and request for a hearing. Complainant indicated that she timely filed hearing requests for her complaints and the Agency was on actual notice of the filings. Complainant argued that the Agency failed to respond and therefore sanctions against the Agency were warranted. Specifically, Complainant stated that she provided a copy of her October 1, 2021, hearing request of Complaint #2 to the EEOP Director on October 6, 2021, via email, as an attachment. Complainant included a copy of her October 6, 2021, email showing it was sent to the EEOP Director, and a Senior EEO Specialist, stating, “Good Afternoon, Here’s your copy of the request for hearing attached above. The formal complaint investigation was completed. I wanted to timely request a hearing.” The email message reflects Complainant attached a copy of the request for hearing on Complaint #2. On June 30, 2022, the AJ issued an Order of Dismissal of Complainant’s hearing requests for her complaints. Specifically, the AJ stated that since Complainant filed an appeal of the consolidated final Agency decision, the AJ no longer had jurisdiction over the complaints.

On March 24, 2022, the Agency filed a separate response to each Notice of Intent to Sanction, indicating that sanctions against the Agency were not warranted because it was not served with a notice that Complainant filed a hearing request, and it was not on notice of any order or other requirement until March 10, 2022. Specifically, the Agency stated that Complainant did not use Request for a Hearing Form that was provided to her when the report of investigation was transmitted to her. In that form, Complainant was informed to choose the Agency, in EEOC Public Portal, as “DoD Office of Secretary/Washington Headquarters Services.” Instead, Complainant used an outdated version of Request for a Hearing Form which did not indicate an option to request a hearing in the EEOC Public Portal and thus no instruction choosing the Agency therein. The Agency stated that Complainant’s hearings were docketed, via EEOC Public Portal, with the Agency as “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” on October 6, 2021. At that time, the Agency EEO Program Director (“EEOP Director”) or the Agency’s EEO office did not have access to “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” via FedSEP and thus, the Agency never received the October 6, 2021, filings. The Agency indicated that on March 10, 2022, the EEOP Director requested and received access to the “DoD Armed Forces Retirement Home” FedSEP box as a stopgap measure while discussing with individuals at the EEOC (Office of Federal Operations and Washington Field Office) other ways to ensure more effective usage of FedSEP, given the large population, consisting of multiple agencies, serviced by “DoD Office of Secretary/Washington Headquarters Services.” On March 10, 2022, the EEOP Director promptly uploaded a copy of the final Agency decision in FedSEP, and on March 11, 2022, the Agency counsel requested an extension to respond to the AJ’s Notice of Intent to Sanction. The Agency argued that the AJ should dismiss Complainant’s hearing requests because they were not properly filed. The Agency indicated that Complainant did not send a copy of the hearing requests to the Agency’s EEO office as instructed and as such it properly issued a final Agency decision for both complaints. The Agency stated that Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision and the AJ proceeding with a hearing would be inappropriate. Further, the Agency stated that the AJ lacked jurisdiction to hear Complainant’s complaints because Complainant filed her hearing requests prematurely before her receipt of the investigative report and before 180 days had elapsed under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(h). The Agency indicated that regarding Complaint #1, filed on April 5, 2021, Complainant’s hearing request form was dated September 30, 2021, i.e., before she received the reissued investigative report on October 14, 2021, and before 180 days had elapsed from the filing of the complaint. Regarding Complaint #2, filed on July 9, 2021, the Agency stated that Complainant’s hearing request form was dated October 1, 2021, i.e., before she received the investigative report on November 10, 2021, and only 84 days after the filing of a formal complaint. Based on the foregoing, the Agency asked the AJ to withdraw the Notice of Intent to Sanction the Agency and dismiss Complainant’s hearing requests as they were not properly filed and because the AJ lacked jurisdiction. On May 6, 2022, Complainant submitted to the AJ a motion, in part, to consolidate cases, motion for sanctions, and request for a hearing. Complainant indicated that she timely filed hearing requests for her complaints and the Agency was on actual notice of the filings. Complainant argued that the Agency failed to respond and therefore sanctions against the Agency were warranted. Specifically, Complainant stated that she provided a copy of her October 1, 2021, hearing request of Complaint #2 to the EEOP Director on October 6, 2021, via email, as an attachment. Complainant included a copy of her October 6, 2021, email showing it was sent to the EEOP Director, and a Senior EEO Specialist, stating, “Good Afternoon, Here’s your copy of the request for hearing attached above. The formal complaint investigation was completed. I wanted to timely request a hearing.” The email message reflects Complainant attached a copy of the request for hearing on Complaint #2. On June 30, 2022, the AJ issued an Order of Dismissal of Complainant’s hearing requests for her complaints. Specifically, the AJ stated that since Complainant filed an appeal of the consolidated final Agency decision, the AJ no longer had jurisdiction over the complaints.

From July 2019 to January 2020, Contract Project Manager, Armed Forces Retirement Home, yelled at her while on site visits, and made comments, such as, “I’m sick of [Complainant],” “[Complainant] gets on my nerves,” and “Watch out for [Complainant].” 4. On January 14, 2020, her supervisor (S1), Chief, Resident Services, GS-14, instructed her to send emails upon her arrival and departure from work. 5. On January 17, 2020, S1 removed her as the Contracting Surveillance Representative for Global Connections to Employment duties. 6. On January 17, 2020, September 30, 2019, and June 2, 2019, S1 issued her Letters of Counseling. 7. In March and July 2020, S1 denied her request for telework and hazard pay. 8. In July 2020, S1 issued her a rating of 1 (Unsatisfactory) for Fiscal Year 2020 after revising her Strategic Goal performance element without notice or her participating in her performance plans. 9. On December 15, 2020, S1 threatened to demote her, removed her Contract Officer Representative duties, and “put [her] in a corner” of the office. 10. On January 11, 2021, S1 placed her on an Opportunity to Improve. 11. On January 21, 2021, she was made aware Human Resources did not process her union dues for six months and refused to provide the union’s correct contact information. 12. In February 2021, Senior Financial Analyst, Armed Forces Retirement Home, sent emails and text messages with rude slurs, sexual graphics, and asking the question, “How’s life on the plantation.” 13. On March 24, 2021, Human Resources Specialist denied her request for tuition reimbursement stating the Agency does not have a tuition reimbursement program. The Agency dismissed the discrete portion of claims 4 – 8 due to untimely EEO Counselor contact pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(2) but accepted those as part of the hostile work environment claim. The Agency also dismissed Complainant’s alleged basis of reprisal because her filing a complaint against Human Resources office for not posting union representatives contact information did not constitute protected activity within the meaning of the EEO regulations. On an unspecified date, she was denied a promotion. 2. On unspecified dates, she was excluded from staff activities. 3. From July 2019 to January 2020, Contract Project Manager, Armed Forces Retirement Home, yelled at her while on site visits, and made comments, such as, “I’m sick of [Complainant],” “[Complainant] gets on my nerves,” and “Watch out for [Complainant].” 4. On January 14, 2020, her supervisor (S1), Chief, Resident Services, GS-14, instructed her to send emails upon her arrival and departure from work. 5. On January 17, 2020, S1 removed her as the Contracting Surveillance Representative for Global Connections to Employment duties. 6. On January 17, 2020, September 30, 2019, and June 2, 2019, S1 issued her Letters of Counseling. 7. In March and July 2020, an individual denied her request for telework and hazard pay. 8. In July 2020, S1 issued her a rating of 1 (Unsatisfactory) for Fiscal Year 2020 after revising her Strategic Goal performance element without notice or her participating in her performance plans. 9. On December 15, 2020, S1 threatened to demote her, removed her Contract Officer Representative duties, and “put [her] in a corner” of the office. 10. On January 11, 2021, S1 placed her on an Opportunity to Improve. 11. On January 21, 2021, she was made aware Human Resources did not process her union dues for six months and refused to provide the union’s correct contact information. 12. In February 2021, Senior Financial Analyst, Armed Forces Retirement Home, sent emails and text messages with rude slurs, sexual graphics, and asking the question, “How’s life on the plantation.” 13. On March 24, 2021, Human Resources Specialist denied her request for tuition reimbursement stating the Agency does not have a tuition reimbursement program. On June 10, 2021, an individual accepted claims 10 and 13 as discrete acts and accepted claims 4 – 10 and 13 as part of the hostile work environment claim. The an individual dismissed claims 1 and 2, for failure to provide clarifying information and dismissed claims 3, 11, and 12 for failure to state a claim, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.107(a)(7) and .107(a)(1), respectively. The an individual dismissed the discrete portion of claims 4 – 8 due to untimely EEO Counselor contact pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(2) but accepted those as part of the hostile work environment claim. items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Rating Veterans Service Representative at the Agency’s Regional Office facility in North Little Rock, Arkansas. 1. On May 16, 2020, he became aware of his non-selection/failure to promote to the Supervisory Veterans Service Representative, GS-13 position under Vacancy announcement 350-20-DLM-10787513-NBU. 2 Complainant asserted that he was subject to discrimination based on race, age, sex, and reprisal when he was not selected for an interview for a position for which he was well-qualified and the selected candidates, who were younger, white women, were less qualified than he was. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 67-69. He stated that his prior protected activity consists of being interviewed by the Administrative Review Board in a complaint of discriminatory and unfair labor practices and filing a complaint with the Office of Special Counsel. See ROI at 63. The Assistant Veterans Service Center Manager (Assistant Manager), who determined the best qualified candidates from the applicant list and served on the interview panel, stated that the criteria to be deemed best qualified was whether the applicant was meeting or exceeding all elements of their performance standard from October 1, 2019 to March 31, 2020. See ROI at 81. If an applicant was not meeting or exceeding all elements of their performance standards, they were deemed to be not best qualified. See ROI at 81. She stated that she found Complainant not to be best qualified because he was not meeting all elements of his performance standards during the relevant time. See ROI at 83. Complainant’s recent performance appraisal rated Complainant as not meeting the goal of Fully Successful on the Quality element of his evaluation. See ROI at 204-207. The Assistant Manager explained that the best qualified candidates were then scored and ranked based on their resume, previous supervisory experience, interview questions, and a written exercise. See ROI at 83. She further stated that of the two selectees, one had extensive supervisory experience within the Agency and while the other did not have previous supervisory experience, both selectees demonstrated through the interview and the written exercise a high likelihood of success in the position. See ROI at 84. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). the decision found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for not selecting Complainant for the position and that Complainant did not submit evidence to support his assertions of discriminatory animus. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed, arguing that the Agency’s explanations of its actions was untrue and should not have been accepted. In response, the Agency urges affirmance of its final decision. The Agency dismissed Complainant’s allegation that the Agency subjected him to a hostile work environment between March 8, 2019 and October 2019 for untimely counselor contact. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 35-37.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Nuclear Medicine Physician, GS-15, with the Imaging Service for the Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Martinsburg, West Virginia. On March 30, 2017, Complainant contacted an EEO Counselor regarding unlawful discrimination and a hostile work environment. On May 4, 2017, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected her to discrimination and a hostile work environment based on religion (Muslim) and sex (female). On June 21, 2017, the Agency issued a Notice of Partial Acceptance on Complainant’s complaint noting she alleged that she was subjected to a hostile work environment based on religion (Muslim) and sex (female) consisting of 15 separate events. The Agency found four of the events listed were timely raised discrete acts and accepted them for investigation as independently actionable claims of disparate treatment (events 1, 13, 14, and 15). Complainant filed an objection to the Notice of Partial Acceptance. On July 27, 2017, the Agency issued a Response to Disagreement with Notice of Partial Acceptance noting Complainant disagreed with the framing of four of the events listed, and requested to add the basis of retaliation to her complaint. The Agency stated it would make the changes necessary as stated in Complainant’s disagreement letter and issue a new notice of partial acceptance. A Revised Notice of Partial Acceptance was issued on July 27, 2017, framing Complainant’s complaint as alleging she was subjected to a hostile work environment based on religion (Muslim), disability, sex (female), and in reprisal for protected EEO activity as evidenced by fifteen events. The Agency accepted five events for investigation as independently actionable claims of disparate treatment (events 1, 12, 13, 14, and 15) and stated that all the events would be considered as part of Complainant’s overall harassment claim. Complainant filed an amendment to her complaint dated July 26, 2017. Complainant requested the following two events be added to her complaint: on June 30, 2017, the Agency summarily suspended Complainant’s clinical privileges and notified her that it is considering permanently revoking her clinical privileges; and on July 10, 2017, the Agency initiated a summary review of Complainant’s employment as a probationary employee. Complainant stated these two events were a direct continuation of the pattern and practice of harassment previously raised. Further, she noted the harassment had escalated, “with the termination of [her] employment and revocation of her clinical privileges now the apparent goal.” Complainant argued the new claims were like or related to those raising during counseling and should be added to the claims already accepted for investigation. On July 27, 2017, the Agency issued a Notice of Amendment of the EEO Complaint, acknowledging receipt of Complainant’s amendment. The Notice stated that the current accepted claim, as indicated in the Revised Notice of Partial Acceptance letter dated July 27, 2017, is one of hostile work environment consisting of 15 events and five disparate treatment claims. The Notice acknowledged that on July 26, 2017, Complainant requested her complaint be amended to include two additional events based on religion and sex. On March 30 and 31, 2017, Supervisor communicated in an angry tone “you only want to win. I'm done with you” after Complainant voiced her concerns about appropriate patients released processes. 11. In April 2017, during a Human Resource meeting with Chief, Complainant’s personal medical information was disclosed to the group. 13. On April 24, 2017, Complainant’s credential file was not presented during a meeting which caused a delay in her renewal privileges. 14. items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Clerk at the Agency’s Florissant Post Office in Jefferson City, Missouri. Supervisor Customer Service (Supervisor) was his first-level supervisor. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 92. 1. On February 2, 2021, he was issued a letter of warning; and 2. On February 27, 2021, his work hours were changed. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ assigned to the case issued a Notice of Proposed Judgment (Notice) indicating his intent to issue a decision without a hearing. Subsequently, the AJ determined that the complaint did not warrant a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on February 18, 2022, incorporating the reasons provided in the Notice. The AJ found that the Agency provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for each of the claims. As to claim 1, Supervisor issued Complainant a Letter of Warning for failing to maintain a regular work schedule, based upon Complainant’s failure to report to work on a day that he was scheduled to work. As to claim 2, Supervisor asserted that Complainant’s duty hours were changed for operational reasons. Specifically, Supervisor said that Complainant was best qualified to process certain mail parcels that did not arrive at the facility until later than his prior start time. Turning to Complainant to establish that the Agency’s reasons were pretext for discrimination, the AJ found that Complainant did not do so. Concerning claim 1, the AJ noted that Complainant claimed that the Letter of Warning was issued because of “personal” reasons and the only reason provided to him was “rules and regulations.” The AJ noted that Complainant asserted that his medical condition was the reason for the Agency’s action because Supervisor “mentioned,” however, Complainant did not explicitly state what Supervisor said or explain how his medical condition was referenced. As such, the AJ determined that this alone was insufficient to demonstrate that the Agency’s reason was pretext for discrimination based on his disability. As to claim 2, the AJ noted that Complainant asserted that Supervisor changed his work hours because he did not follow her instructions. The AJ found that, even if that was correct, that is insufficient to prove pretext. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Complainant did not provide arguments in support of his appeal. The Agency contends that the AJ’s decision was proper and their decision implementing it should stand.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Supervisory Emergency Management Specialist, GS-0089-15, Information Technology Service Division, Office of Resource Management at the Agency’s Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response (OASPR or ASPR) in Washington D.C. 1. On September 19, 2018, he requested the OASPR Human Resources leadership investigate harassment (non-sexual) claims that were reported by anonymous employees. Whether he was subjected to discrimination and harassment (non-sexual) on the bases of sex (male), age (over 40), and in reprisal for opposing an unlawful discriminatory practice when: 2. On December 7, 2018, the Agency assigned him to the Cybersecurity Advisor, GS-15, position effective December 10, 2018. 3. On December 10, 2018, he learned that management had impeded his ability to compete for the Director, Office of Security, Intelligence, and Information Management (SIIM), GS-15, position. 4. On January 7, 2019, he learned that the Agency selected another employee outside of the Agency as the Director, SIIM, GS-15, position. 5. a. In November 2018, and ongoing, management impeded his ability to compete for a SES (Senior Executive Service) position. b. On December 4, 2018, OASPR management subjected him to coercive and threatening behavior. c. On December 10, 2018, and ongoing, OASPR management removed him from participating on the ASPR Senior Leadership Team. d. On January 7, 2019, the Agency informed him that he would be moving from his window office on the fifth floor to the building’s basement. Complainant has not challenged the Agency’s framing of the complaint. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before EEOC Administrative Judge or a final Agency decision. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). Complainant requested a final Agency decision without a hearing. The Agency issued a final decision finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The Agency dismissed claim 1 for failure to state a claim since it involved unidentified employees and not Complainant. Regarding claims 2 and 5b, the record reveals that in 2018, OASPR went through a realignment of staff. As a result, OASPR employees were reassigned based on the organization’s needs. The record indicates that during the realignment period, Complainant was detailed to the Acting SIIM Director position. Complainant does not claim this detail was discriminatory. Complainant’s second-level supervisor (S2), Assistant Secretary for OASPR, a political appointee, stated that in July - fall 2018, an Associate Deputy proposed Complainant’s detail to a Cybersecurity Advisor position. On December 3, 2018, S2 met with Complainant and offered Complainant the Cybersecurity Advisor position that was proposed by the Associate Deputy. S2 indicated that based on Complainant’s resume, Complainant had very deep cybersecurity experience. Complainant told S2 that he would think about the offer. S2 stated that on December 4, 2018, S2 stopped by Complainant’s office but Complainant was angry and hostile and told S2 that he was not interested in the Cybersecurity Advisor position because he was not an expert in the field and expressed his interest in applying for a SIIM Director, SES, position instead. S2 told Complainant that the SIIM Director position was not a SES position rather it was a GS-15 position. The record indicates that on December 7, 2018, Complainant’s first-level supervisor (S1), an SES, Deputy Assistant Secretary, issued Complainant a notice of his reassignment to the Cybersecurity Advisor, GS-15, position due to the organization consolidation and prioritization of cybersecurity. S1 indicated that Complainant was being reassigned in order to meet the needs of the organization as well as taking into consideration Complainant’s background and qualifications. The notice indicated that there would be no change to Complainant’s position description. The record indicates that Complainant’s position title remained as a Supervisory Emergency Management Specialist, GS-15. Complainant’s coworker (C1), female, a GS-15 employee, position title unknown, at the Incident Management Team Program, indicated that in 2018, OASPR went through a realignment of positions. As a result of the realignment, C1 stated, employees were reassigned to different positions, some employees were allowed to choose and some employees, including C1, were assigned to positions they were not qualified for, placing them outside the scope of their pre- alignment position description. C1 indicated that as a result of the realignment, she was reassigned to the Intel Division which did not align with her abilities. The Chief of Staff, SES, OASPR, indicated that Complainant was serving as the Acting SIIM Director prior to his reassignment to the Cybersecurity Advisor position and management lost confidence in his ability to serve in that Acting position. The Chief of Staff stated that since Complainant had cybersecurity talents and expertise, he was best used to improve OASPR’s cyber capabilities which were lacking. Regarding claims 3, 4, and 5a, S1 and S2 indicated that no one impeded Complainant’s ability to compete for the SIIM Director position or an SES position. The HR Director indicated that she was a selecting official for the SIIM Director, GS-15 position at issue. The HR Director stated that there was no vacancy announcement created for the position; rather, under the Agency’s merit promotion plan, she utilized a shared certificate, which was a list of candidates eligible for the position posted in another Agency. The HR Director noted that the shared certificate process was very popular because HR had a lot of turn over, and they were taking a long time to get vacancy announcements posted. Complainant had not applied for a particular position at another agency and thus was not on the shared certificate. Therefore, Complainant was never considered for the position. The HR Director indicated that she selected a female (Selectee), from outside the Agency, for the SIIM Director position. Regarding claim 5c, S2 indicated that since Complainant was reassigned to the Senior Cybersecurity Advisor position, he did not need to participate on the OASPR Senior Leadership Team meetings. The an individual of Staff, SES, OASPR, indicated that Complainant was serving as the Acting SIIM Director prior to his reassignment to the Cybersecurity Advisor position and management lost confidence in his ability to serve in that Acting position. The an individual of Staff stated that since Complainant had cybersecurity talents and expertise, he was best used to improve OASPR’s cyber capabilities which were lacking. Regarding claims 3, 4, and 5a, an individual and S2 indicated that no one impeded Complainant’s ability to compete for the SIIM Director position or an SES position. The an individualDirector indicated that she was a selecting official for the SIIM Director, GS-15 position at issue. The an individualDirector stated that there was no vacancy announcement created for the position; rather, under the Agency’s merit promotion plan, she utilized a shared certificate, which was a list of candidates eligible for the position posted in another Agency. The an individualDirector noted that the shared certificate process was very popular because HR had a lot of turn over, and they were taking a long time to get vacancy announcements posted. Complainant had not applied for a particular position at another agency and thus was not on the shared certificate. Therefore, Complainant was never considered for the position. The an individualDirector indicated that she selected a female (Selectee), from outside the Agency, for the SIIM Director position. Regarding claim 5c, an individual indicated that since Complainant was reassigned to the Senior Cybersecurity Advisor position, he did not need to participate on the OASPR Senior Leadership Team meetings. Regarding claim 5d, an individual stated that due to Complainant’s reassignment to the Senior Cybersecurity Advisor position, his office was also changed to the floor where everyone within his new office was located. Based on the foregoing, the Agency issued its decision finding that an individual failed to establish discrimination as alleged. On appeal, Complainant requests that the Commission sanction the Agency by issuing a default judgment due to the Agency’s failure to issue a final decision in a timely manner. an individual indicates that although he requested a final decision on September 17, 2019, he did not receive a final Agency decision until September 21, 2021. an individual states that the Agency’s delay caused him harm to his career and emotional distress. In response to an individual’s appeal, the Agency acknowledges that it took more than 60 days to issue a final decision as required by 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). However, an individual states that it has not acted in a manner that would warrant a default judgment and Complainant has not demonstrated that he has been prejudiced by the delay.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Senior Resident Agent at the Agency’s Roanoke Resident Agency in Roanoke, Virginia. On November 2, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (Asian) and sex (male) when: 1. On September 10, 2020, Complainant became aware that the Agency did not select him for a promotion to the Assistant to the Special Agent in Charge (ASAIC) position, GS-181-14, Office of Investigations (OI), Forensic Services Division (FSD) – National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) advertised under Vacancy Announcement Number VAN) 20148. 2. On September 10, 2020, Complainant became aware that the Agency did not select him for a promotion to the ASAIC position, GS-1811-14, OI, London Resident Office- Paris Field Office advertised under VAN 20151. 3. On September 10, 2020, Complainant became aware that the Agency did not select him for a promotion to the ASAIC position, GS-1811-14, OI, Pittsburgh Field Office, advertised under VAN 20155. 4. On September 24, 2020, Complainant became aware that the Agency omitted a Statement of Qualifications Requirement (SOQ) from the OI, FSD, NCMEC, advertised under VAN 20148. 5. On September 24, 2020, Complainant became aware that the ASAIC position, GS-1411-14, OI, FSD, NCMEC, advertised under VAN 16095, for which he applied for between June 15 through 29, 2016, was predetermined to be filled by a Caucasian female. 2 Complainant asserts that he is more qualified than any of the Selectees for the positions. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 227-28; 230. He further contends that removing the SOQ from the vacancy announcement in claim 4 allowed for multiple bids from individuals who would not otherwise have been qualified and if the SOQ had been included, that he would have been the only applicant who had held the exact position for three years. See ROI at 230-31. The Assistant Director, who was the selecting official, stated that each of the Selectees for the positions was recommended as the best qualified for the position and his general practice is to choose a candidate from those recommended by the Special Agent in Charge (SAIC) for the vacancy. See ROI at 235-38. The Division Chief stated that SOQ’s are not mandatory and are at the discretion of the directorate soliciting for the vacancy. See ROI at 252. The Special Agent in Charge for the vacancy in claim 1 stated that he recommended that the directorate not include a SOQ because it was not necessary as the qualifications were commensurate with any GS-14 supervisor position. See ROI at 256-57. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision dismissed claim 5 pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(2) for untimely counselor contact, finding Complainant did not contact an EEO counselor until four years after the discriminatory incident. 3 Complainant’s formal complaint indicated race and sex/gender identity as the bases. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 20. We find upon a review of the record that Complainant intended to raise race (Asian) and sex (male) as the bases. We note that the Agency’s decision inadvertently stated that it was dismissing claim 4 for untimely counselor contact but the decision makes it clear that it was claim 5 that was dismissed. The decision went on to find that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for all of the non-selections and for omitting the SOQ from the posting in claim 4, and that Complainant did not establish that the Agency’s reasons were a pretext for discrimination. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision. In response, the Agency filed a brief urging affirmance of its decision.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant was a Vocational Trade Instructor, GS-1712-11, at the Agency’s U.S. Penitentiary in Atwater, California. On June 11, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), sex (female), parental status (parent) 2, and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when, on April 10, 2019, her supervisor requested a doctor's note due to the utilization of leave from a work-place injury. The Commission does not have jurisdiction over claims of parental status discrimination. Moran v. Dep't of Veterans Affairs, EEOC [number removed] (Oct. 8, 2002). Accordingly, we will not address parental status as a basis herein. Complainant averred that she was the only African-American woman in her unit. Report of Investigation (ROI), p. 87. She reported to the Supervisor of Education (S1) (Hispanic female, no prior EEO activity, married with children). Her second-level supervisor was the Associate Warden (S2) (Caucasian female, no prior EEO activity). Her third-level supervisor was the Acting Warden (S3) (White male, prior EEO). On April 9, 2019, Complainant requested to extend her LWOP to June 1, 2019, via an email, which she copied to the Human Resources Manager and the Union President. Report of Investigation (ROI), pp. 84, 86. In her request, she attached two notes from her doctor, that stated she would be out through June 1, 2019. At the time of the incident, Complainant was not at work and had been on approved leave after she had sustained a work injury on October 2, 2018. On April 10, 2019, S1 sent Complainant an email in which she asked Complainant to obtain a doctor’s prognosis and diagnosis of her medical condition and to send that to S1, but S1 denied that she asked for the information via email. Complainant questioned the supervisor’s request as to the reasons why she was requesting medical documentation. Complainant stated that this was not the normal protocol as management had granted her previous requests to extend her leave without the submission of any additional medical documentation. S1 told Complainant that the Region had requested the information. ROI, p. 173. After Complainant asked additional questions, S1 referred Complainant to S3 for further information. 3 S3 told Complainant that no one in the Regional Office was requesting additional information and he did not know why S1 was requesting the information. S3 also told her that he would approve her request to extend her LWOP without submitting additional documentation. S3 stated that he believed this had been a miscommunication issue. According to Complainant, Complainant’s request to extend LWOP was subsequently approved. Complainant expressed her belief that her supervisor had committed a violation of the Health Information Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). 4 ROI, p. 84. Complainant stated her doctor already provided a note stating she should be out of work. Complainant did not understand why that was not good enough. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. This appeal followed. The record shows that S2 was on leave from April 8, 2019 to April 12, 2019. ROI, p. 103. The Commission does not have jurisdiction over HIPAA claims. HIPAA is enforced by the Department of Health and Human Services.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Food Service Worker, WG-7408-02, at the Agency’s William S. Middleton Memorial VA Hospital in Madison, Wisconsin. On May 29, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the basis of age (78) when, on April 19, 2019, Complainant was terminated from his probationary position. Complainant entered duty on December 26, 2018, on a one-year probationary period. Report of Investigation (ROI), p. 148. His immediate supervisor was the Food Service Supervisor, WS-4 (age 33) (S1). S1 averred he did not know Complainant’s specific age, but he guessed he was in his early 70’s. Tab 7-2, p. 86. S1 testified that, on April 11, 2019, another coworker reported that he observed Complainant eating the Department’s food (a hamburger) and reported it to S1, who stated he observed Complainant eating something. ROI, p. 71. Complainant denied eating the Department food, which is considered theft. Complainant claimed that he was falsely accused of eating food from a patient’s tray. Complainant stated the food was described as a hamburger, but there were no hamburgers on the menu that day, and he stated, “I don’t eat meat.” ROI, p. 38. S1 acknowledged that hamburgers were not on the menu on the day in question, but S1 averred there may have been an extra one on the cart because it was easier to have the sandwich assembled on the cart when requested by a veteran. S1 stated this is not the first time that employees reported Complainant eating the Department’s food. Complainant later acknowledged that he ate an apple turnover. ROI, p. 71. Complainant had previously received a letter of written counseling for failing to complete his assigned duties and to follow the nutrition and food service policies. Complainant’s third level supervisor, the Chief, Nutrition and Food Services, GS-14 (age 36), (S3) recommended Complainant’s termination. ROI, pp. 70-71, 76-77, and 190. S3 averred she was not aware of Complainant’s age. ROI, pp.71-72. She stated she had terminated another younger person for eating the Department food. The Chief, Human Resources (S2) was the signatory to the decision, which was issued to Complainant on April 19, 2019. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Management Analyst, GS-09, at the Agency's Human Resources Liaison Data Branch, Office of Management Technology and Operations, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration facility in Rockville, Maryland. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 68. According to Complainant, on June 30, 2016, she met with her first-level supervisor (Supervisor) who told her that she was not receiving a promotion because she was not working independently; relied too heavily on her partner; made too many errors; could not handle complicated work; and was not working at the higher-grade level. ROI at 202. Complainant stated that Supervisor wanted her to demonstrate that she was capable of handling work at the higher grade for six months before Supervisor would consider a promotion. Id. In response, Supervisor explained that Complainant met the time and grade requirements to be eligible for a career ladder promotion but her performance, at that time, did not demonstrate the potential to perform the duties at the GS-11 grade-level. Id. at 305. Supervisor added that she issued Complainant a career ladder memorandum indicating specific areas of improvement that she would assess in another six months. Id. Supervisor averred that Complainant was nevertheless promoted to the GS-11 grade-level at the conclusion of her six-month review period on January 8, 2017. Id. Complainant’s second-level supervisor, the Director of Division of Management Services (Director), stated that she was aware that Complainant's career ladder promotion was being delayed until her performance was at the level where she would be eligible. Director averred that Supervisor created a six-month performance plan for Complainant, which she has done for other staff members. Id. at 567. Director explained that performance plans are a common management practice to help employees reach promotion objectives. Id. She affirmed that Complainant fulfilled the requirements of her performance plan and has since been promoted. Id. In her rebuttal, Complainant argued that Supervisor did not address her performance issues prior to June 30, 2016. She also stated that the only other employee issued a performance plan by Supervisor was her coworker (Coworker) (male, Puerto Rican). Id. at 279. But he only had to demonstrate performance at a higher-level for two months after becoming eligible prior to receiving his promotion. Id. According to Supervisor, Complainant was promoted to the Management Analyst, GS-11, position to perform Human Resources (HR) Liaison Duties at the Full Performance Level (FPL) of GS-12 on January 8, 2017, and Coworker was promoted on December 11, 2016, with the FPL of GS-11. Supplemental Report of Investigation (Supp. ROI) at 29. On November 7, 2016, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging 25 claims of discrimination and harassment on the bases of national origin (Mexican), disability (perceived mental), age (52), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. 2 Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge. In accordance with Complainant's request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. In EEOC [number removed] (Sept. 19, 2019), 3 we affirmed the Agency’s decision finding of no discrimination with the exception of the duplicate claims of 3 and 25 wherein Complainant alleged that she was denied a promotion to the position of Management Analyst, GS-11, on June Complainant maintained that her August 8, 2016, EEO Counselor contact constituted as her prior protected EEO activity with regard to the instant complaint. However, the record reflects that Complainant first contacted the Agency’s EEO office on July 26, 2016. ROI at 69. We denied the Agency’s request for reconsideration in EEOC [number removed] (May 8, 2020). 30, 2016. We found that the record was not fully developed with regard to the promotion allegation, and therefore remanded the duplicate claims 3 and 25 for the Agency to conduct a supplemental investigation and issue a new final decision addressing the merits of these claims. We specifically noted that the Agency's investigation did not address Complainant's specific assertion that, where she was required to demonstrate higher-level performance over a six-month period, Coworker only had to demonstrate a higher-level performance for two months before being promoted to the Management Analyst position at the GS-11 grade-level. As such, we ordered the Agency to conduct a supplemental investigation to: 1. [O]btain an affidavit from Supervisor or another person with knowledge, indicating when Coworker was promoted; whether he was only required to complete a two- month evaluation period; and, if so, why his evaluation period was only two months while Complainant was required to complete a six-month period; and 2. [P]rovide documentation establishing the exact promotion dates of both Complainant and Coworker to GS-11, Management Analyst. The Agency subsequently issued Complainant a copy of its completed supplemental report of investigation, and thereafter issued its second final decision, addressing claims 3 and 25. In its final decision, the Agency found that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case of discrimination with respect to any of her protected classes and did not show that its legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons were pretextual or that it was motivated by discriminatory or retaliatory animus. In so finding, the Agency explained that six months prior to when Coworker became eligible for promotion on October 2, 2016, an evaluation plan was created for him to ensure that he was meeting the established milestones to be promoted. The Agency noted that when Coworker became eligible for promotion, a two-month evaluation period was then added to ensure that he could fulfill the performance of the position. The Agency also noted that Complainant was nevertheless promoted to the Management Analyst, GS-11, position at the conclusion of her six-month review period on January 8, 2017. The Agency further observed that Complainant was performing HR Liaison duties before her promotion, while Coworker held a non-HR Liaison position before his promotion to the Management Analyst, GS-11, position. The Agency found that Complainant’s and Coworker’s duties and positions were not the same, and that they received a fair assessment of their readiness for promotion.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant was a Vocational Trade Instructor, GS-1712-11, at the Agency’s U.S. Penitentiary in Atwater, California. On June 11, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), sex (female), parental status (parent) 2, and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when, on April 10, 2019, her supervisor requested a doctor's note due to the utilization of leave from a work-place injury. The Commission does not have jurisdiction over claims of parental status discrimination. Moran v. Dep't of Veterans Affairs, EEOC [number removed] (Oct. 8, 2002). Accordingly, we will not address parental status as a basis herein. Complainant averred that she was the only African-American woman in her unit. Report of Investigation (ROI), p. 87. She reported to the Supervisor of Education (S1) (Hispanic female, no prior EEO activity, married with children). Her second-level supervisor was the Associate Warden (S2) (Caucasian female, no prior EEO activity). Her third-level supervisor was the Acting Warden (S3) (White male, prior EEO). On April 9, 2019, Complainant requested to extend her LWOP to June 1, 2019, via an email, which she copied to the Human Resources Manager and the Union President. Report of Investigation (ROI), pp. 84, 86. In her request, she attached two notes from her doctor, that stated she would be out through June 1, 2019. At the time of the incident, Complainant was not at work and had been on approved leave after she had sustained a work injury on October 2, 2018. On April 10, 2019, S1 sent Complainant an email in which she asked Complainant to obtain a doctor’s prognosis and diagnosis of her medical condition and to send that to S1, but S1 denied that she asked for the information via email. Complainant questioned the supervisor’s request as to the reasons why she was requesting medical documentation. Complainant stated that this was not the normal protocol as management had granted her previous requests to extend her leave without the submission of any additional medical documentation. S1 told Complainant that the Region had requested the information. ROI, p. 173. After Complainant asked additional questions, S1 referred Complainant to S3 for further information. 3 S3 told Complainant that no one in the Regional Office was requesting additional information and he did not know why S1 was requesting the information. S3 also told her that he would approve her request to extend her LWOP without submitting additional documentation. S3 stated that he believed this had been a miscommunication issue. According to Complainant, Complainant’s request to extend LWOP was subsequently approved. Complainant expressed her belief that her supervisor had committed a violation of the Health Information Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). 4 ROI, p. 84. Complainant stated her doctor already provided a note stating she should be out of work. Complainant did not understand why that was not good enough. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. This appeal followed. The record shows that S2 was on leave from April 8, 2019 to April 12, 2019. ROI, p. 103. The Commission does not have jurisdiction over HIPAA claims. HIPAA is enforced by the Department of Health and Human Services.

Middleton Memorial VA Hospital in Madison, Wisconsin. Complainant entered duty on December 26, 2018, on a one-year probationary period. Report of Investigation (ROI), p. 148. His immediate supervisor was the Food Service Supervisor, WS-4 (age 33) (S1). S1 averred he did not know Complainant’s specific age, but he guessed he was in his early 70’s. Tab 7-2, p. 86.
