items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Management Analyst, GS-09, at the Agency's Human Resources Liaison Data Branch, Office of Management Technology and Operations, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration facility in Rockville, Maryland. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 68. According to Complainant, on June 30, 2016, she met with her first-level supervisor (Supervisor) who told her that she was not receiving a promotion because she was not working independently; relied too heavily on her partner; made too many errors; could not handle complicated work; and was not working at the higher-grade level. ROI at 202. Complainant stated that Supervisor wanted her to demonstrate that she was capable of handling work at the higher grade for six months before Supervisor would consider a promotion. Id. In response, Supervisor explained that Complainant met the time and grade requirements to be eligible for a career ladder promotion but her performance, at that time, did not demonstrate the potential to perform the duties at the GS-11 grade-level. Id. at 305. Supervisor added that she issued Complainant a career ladder memorandum indicating specific areas of improvement that she would assess in another six months. Id. Supervisor averred that Complainant was nevertheless promoted to the GS-11 grade-level at the conclusion of her six-month review period on January 8, 2017. Id. Complainant’s second-level supervisor, the Director of Division of Management Services (Director), stated that she was aware that Complainant's career ladder promotion was being delayed until her performance was at the level where she would be eligible. Director averred that Supervisor created a six-month performance plan for Complainant, which she has done for other staff members. Id. at 567. Director explained that performance plans are a common management practice to help employees reach promotion objectives. Id. She affirmed that Complainant fulfilled the requirements of her performance plan and has since been promoted. Id. In her rebuttal, Complainant argued that Supervisor did not address her performance issues prior to June 30, 2016. She also stated that the only other employee issued a performance plan by Supervisor was her coworker (Coworker) (male, Puerto Rican). Id. at 279. But he only had to demonstrate performance at a higher-level for two months after becoming eligible prior to receiving his promotion. Id. According to Supervisor, Complainant was promoted to the Management Analyst, GS-11, position to perform Human Resources (HR) Liaison Duties at the Full Performance Level (FPL) of GS-12 on January 8, 2017, and Coworker was promoted on December 11, 2016, with the FPL of GS-11. Supplemental Report of Investigation (Supp. ROI) at 29. On November 7, 2016, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging 25 claims of discrimination and harassment on the bases of national origin (Mexican), disability (perceived mental), age (52), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. 2 Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge. In accordance with Complainant's request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. In EEOC [number removed] (Sept. 19, 2019), 3 we affirmed the Agency’s decision finding of no discrimination with the exception of the duplicate claims of 3 and 25 wherein Complainant alleged that she was denied a promotion to the position of Management Analyst, GS-11, on June Complainant maintained that her August 8, 2016, EEO Counselor contact constituted as her prior protected EEO activity with regard to the instant complaint. However, the record reflects that Complainant first contacted the Agency’s EEO office on July 26, 2016. ROI at 69. We denied the Agency’s request for reconsideration in EEOC [number removed] (May 8, 2020). 30, 2016. We found that the record was not fully developed with regard to the promotion allegation, and therefore remanded the duplicate claims 3 and 25 for the Agency to conduct a supplemental investigation and issue a new final decision addressing the merits of these claims. We specifically noted that the Agency's investigation did not address Complainant's specific assertion that, where she was required to demonstrate higher-level performance over a six-month period, Coworker only had to demonstrate a higher-level performance for two months before being promoted to the Management Analyst position at the GS-11 grade-level. As such, we ordered the Agency to conduct a supplemental investigation to: 1. [O]btain an affidavit from Supervisor or another person with knowledge, indicating when Coworker was promoted; whether he was only required to complete a two- month evaluation period; and, if so, why his evaluation period was only two months while Complainant was required to complete a six-month period; and 2. [P]rovide documentation establishing the exact promotion dates of both Complainant and Coworker to GS-11, Management Analyst. The Agency subsequently issued Complainant a copy of its completed supplemental report of investigation, and thereafter issued its second final decision, addressing claims 3 and 25. In its final decision, the Agency found that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case of discrimination with respect to any of her protected classes and did not show that its legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons were pretextual or that it was motivated by discriminatory or retaliatory animus. In so finding, the Agency explained that six months prior to when Coworker became eligible for promotion on October 2, 2016, an evaluation plan was created for him to ensure that he was meeting the established milestones to be promoted. The Agency noted that when Coworker became eligible for promotion, a two-month evaluation period was then added to ensure that he could fulfill the performance of the position. The Agency also noted that Complainant was nevertheless promoted to the Management Analyst, GS-11, position at the conclusion of her six-month review period on January 8, 2017. The Agency further observed that Complainant was performing HR Liaison duties before her promotion, while Coworker held a non-HR Liaison position before his promotion to the Management Analyst, GS-11, position. The Agency found that Complainant’s and Coworker’s duties and positions were not the same, and that they received a fair assessment of their readiness for promotion.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Facility Recall Coordinator, GS-6, within the Agency’s Logistics Service at the Medical Center in Miami, Florida. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 32. According to Complainant, on March 3, 2017, he was instructed to be the backup for the Implant Coordinator, a GS-9 position. ROI, at 88-90. As a result, Complainant was informed that he would assist the Implant Coordinator by picking up the implants from the warehouse, signing for them, and delivering them to the Implant Coordinator's desk. Id. at 134. Complainant, however, believed that there were other employees in the unit, who held a GS-9 grade or higher, that should have been made the backup to the Implant Coordinator instead. Id. at 88-90. Complainant averred that he was never trained as the Implant Coordinator nor ever performed the duties of the position before. Id. Complainant believed his race was a factor in the Agency’s actions because "They promoted everyone that was [B]lack." Id. at 89. He also believed his sexual orientation was a factor, "Because the department secretary is gay, but in [the] closet." Id. As for his EEO activity, Complainant asserted it was a factor "[b]ecause it makes my chief look bad." Id. According to the Chief, Complainant was only asked to provide support to the Implant Coordinator, not perform a full-scale backup role. Id. at 100. The Chief further explained that while there were other GS-9 employees, none were available due staffing shortages. Id. The Assistant Chief also explained that Complainant was not given Implant Coordinator training because he refused to take the training, despite the fact that the role of backup to the Implant Coordinator was part of his Position Description (PD). Id. at 135. The following week, on March 10, 2017, Complainant was taken into custody by the VA Police and denied access to critical departments. Id. at 90-91. Specifically, Complainant attested that he was held in VA Police custody for 45 minutes and lost access to every part of the facility. Id. Complaint described feeling humiliated when he was paraded in front of employees and veterans and had to ask people to allow him into departments. Id. Regarding Complainant’s detention, the Director explained that all staff members were previously informed of the Secretary’s visit to the facility. Id. at 148-149. Security for the visit involved the VA police and local hospital police, who established a secure perimeter for controlled access to the Secretary. Id. According to the Director, Complainant made concerning statements on his Facebook page about the Secretary, which were shared with the security team. Id. On the day of the visit, Complainant entered the secured area dressed in a three-piece suit and provided, what VA Police considered, an unacceptable reason for his presence. Id. The Director attested that Complainant was then escorted off Agency property, where he continued to convey his concerns via Facebook from a location across the street from the Medical Center. Id. Thereafter, the Chief issued Complainant a Proposed 5-day Suspension, dated March 16, 2017, regarding a separate incident from approximately six months earlier. Id. at 225-226. Therein, the Chief charged Complainant with disrespectful, insulting, and racial language in the workplace. Specifically, the Chief noted that on September 20, 2016, a coworker reported that Complainant said, "Black men are lazy and don't want to work," among other similar comments. Id. Complainant was also charged with disrespectful conduct when he failed to lower his voice and refused to leave his Supervisor’s office. Id. The Chief noted that the VA Police were called because Complainant’s Supervisor felt intimidated by Complainant’s conduct. Id. The Proposed 5-day Suspension was then effectuated by the Agency on April 24, through April 28, 2017. Id. at 227. On April 14, 2017, the Chief issued Complainant a Proposed 10-day suspension, charging Complainant with the “Failure to follow supervisory instruction with Leadership and the Director.” Id. at 223-224. According to the Chief, on January 13, 2017, Complainant was provided with a letter reminding him that he must go through his chain-of-command when voicing his concerns about the workplace. Id. Complainant disregarded the letter, stated the Chief, when he emailed the Director, Assistant Director, and the Secretary of the Agency without going through his chain-of-command. Id. Complainant averred that on April 18, 2017, his PD was changed to include more duties and assignments. Id. at 94-95. In response, the Chief explained that he edited Complainant’s PD and sent it to the Classification Department for vetting. Id. at 109-110. The Chief attested that Complainant was the only Recall Coordinator in the unit and, as time progressed, the attention needed to close out recalls decreased. Moreover, noted the Chief, Complainant was only available half the day to assist the team. Id. Similarly, the Assistant Director stated that there were not enough duties to support Complainant working an eight-hour day and the assignment of additional duties addressed the needs of the Logistics Call Center and the Logistics mission. Id. at 180. On June 21, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (Caucasian), sex (male, sexual orientation 2), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. On March 3, 2017, the Assistant Chief instructed him to be the backup for the Implant Coordinator, a GS-9 position. 2. On March 10, 2017, he was “humiliated” when he was taken into custody by VA Police, who also took away his access to critical departments. In Bostock v. Clayton Cty., the Supreme Court held that discrimination based on sexual orientation or transgender status is prohibited under Title VII. 590 U.S. ___, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020); see also Baldwin v. Dep’t of Transp., EEOC [number removed] (July 15, 2015) (an allegation of discrimination based on sexual orientation states a claim of sex discrimination under Title VII because sexual orientation is inherently a sex-based consideration). 3. On March 22, 2017, he was issued a proposed 5-day suspension. 3 4. On April 18, 2017, he was issued a proposed 10-day suspension. 4 5. On April 18, 2017, his Position Description (PD) was changed to “include more duties and assignments.” Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew his request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The Agency specifically found that it articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions regarding claims 1 and 5, which Complainant did not establish were pretextual based on his protected classes. Regarding claim 1, the Agency noted that other GS-9s could not assume the role of backup to the Implant Coordinator due to their workloads, and therefore Complainant was the only employee available to perform the role at the time. The Agency also noted that Complainant did not receive training for the backup responsibilities because he refused to take the training. The Agency reasoned that being the backup to the Implant Coordinator was part of Complainant’s PD when he was hired. Additionally, the Agency noted that when a lower-graded employee is assigned to backup a higher-graded position, as here, they are not performing all the duties of the higher-graded position but are just covering the basic functions. With respect to claim 5, the Agency noted that additional duties were added to Complainant’s PD because his workload as a Recall Coordinator had diminished, leaving him with very little work for half the day. More specifically, the Agency stated that the Recall Coordinator position is typically a collateral duty and most facilities did not have a dedicated Recall Coordinator’s position. In concluding that Complainant did not establish that management’s reasons were pretextual, the Agency noted that Complainant provided no documentation, witness testimony, or other evidence in support of his assertion that his race, sexual orientation, or EEO activity were the reasons for the Agency’s actions. Additionally, the Agency determined that Complainant did not show he was subjected to a hostile work environment based on his protected classes, as alleged. 5 As previously noted, the 5-day suspension was later sustained and effective April 24, through April 28, 2017. The record does not reflect whether the proposed 10-day suspension was subsequently implemented by the Agency. While the Agency did not specifically address claims 2, 3, and 4, in the analysis portion of its decision, they were included in the factual background section. The matters were also part of the Report of Investigation. Consequently, we find there is sufficient evidence in the record for us to In so finding, the Agency noted that Complainant did not establish that the Agency subjected him to unwelcome personal slurs or other denigrating or insulting verbal or physical conduct that was sufficiently severe or pervasive to rise to the level of a hostile work environment. The Agency noted that although Complainant alleged he was called homophobic slurs based on his sexual orientation, he provided no evidence, beyond his own assertions, that he was subjected to any such comments.

The Assistant an individual also explained that Complainant was not given Implant Coordinator training because he refused to take the training, despite the fact that the role of backup to the Implant Coordinator was part of his Position Description (PD). Id. at 135. The following week, on March 10, 2017, Complainant was taken into custody by the VA Police and denied access to critical departments. Id. at 90-91. Specifically, an individual attested that he was held in VA Police custody for 45 minutes and lost access to every part of the facility. Id. Complaint described feeling humiliated when he was paraded in front of employees and veterans and had to ask people to allow him into departments. Id. Regarding an individual’s detention, the Director explained that all staff members were previously informed of the Secretary’s visit to the facility. Id. at 148-149. Security for the visit involved the VA police and local hospital police, who established a secure perimeter for controlled access to the Secretary. Id. According to the Director, Complainant made concerning statements on his Facebook page about the Secretary, which were shared with the security team. Id. On the day of the visit, Complainant entered the secured area dressed in a three-piece suit and provided, what VA Police considered, an unacceptable reason for his presence. Id. The an individual attested that Complainant was then escorted off Agency property, where he continued to convey his concerns via Facebook from a location across the street from the Medical Center. Id. Thereafter, the Chief issued Complainant a Proposed 5-day Suspension, dated March 16, 2017, regarding a separate incident from approximately six months earlier. Id. at 225-226. Therein, the Chief charged Complainant with disrespectful, insulting, and racial language in the workplace. Specifically, the an individual noted that on September 20, 2016, a coworker reported that Complainant said, "Black men are lazy and don't want to work," among other similar comments. Id. Complainant was also charged with disrespectful conduct when he failed to lower his voice and refused to leave his Supervisor’s office. Id. The an individual noted that the VA Police were called because Complainant’s Supervisor felt intimidated by Complainant’s conduct. Id. The Proposed 5-day Suspension was then effectuated by the Agency on April 24, through April 28, 2017. Id. at 227. On April 14, 2017, the Chief issued Complainant a Proposed 10-day suspension, charging Complainant with the “Failure to follow supervisory instruction with Leadership and the Director.” Id. at 223-224. According to the Chief, on January 13, 2017, Complainant was provided with a letter reminding him that he must go through his chain-of-command when voicing his concerns about the workplace. Id. an individual disregarded the letter, stated the Chief, when he emailed the Director, Assistant Director, and the Secretary of the Agency without going through his chain-of-command. Id. an individual averred that on April 18, 2017, his PD was changed to include more duties and assignments. Id. at 94-95. In response, the an individual explained that he edited Complainant’s PD and sent it to the Classification Department for vetting. Id. at 109-110. The an individual attested that Complainant was the only Recall Coordinator in the unit and, as time progressed, the attention needed to close out recalls decreased. Moreover, noted the Chief, Complainant was only available half the day to assist the team. Id. Similarly, the Assistant an individual stated that there were not enough duties to support Complainant working an eight-hour day and the assignment of additional duties addressed the needs of the Logistics Call Center and the Logistics mission. Id. at 180. On June 21, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him on the bases of race (Caucasian), sex (male, sexual orientation 2), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. On March 3, 2017, the Assistant Chief instructed him to be the backup for the Implant Coordinator, a GS-9 position. 2. On March 10, 2017, he was “humiliated” when he was taken into custody by VA Police, who also took away his access to critical departments. In Bostock v. Clayton Cty., the Supreme Court held that discrimination based on sexual orientation or transgender status is prohibited under Title VII. 590 U.S. ___, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020); see also Baldwin v. Dep’t of Transp., EEOC [number removed] (July 15, 2015) (an allegation of discrimination based on sexual orientation states a claim of sex discrimination under Title VII because sexual orientation is inherently a sex-based consideration). 3. On March 22, 2017, he was issued a proposed 5-day suspension. 3 4. On April 18, 2017, he was issued a proposed 10-day suspension. 4 5. On April 18, 2017, his Position Description (PD) was changed to “include more duties and assignments.” Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew his request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that an individual subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The Agency specifically found that it articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions regarding claims 1 and 5, which Complainant did not establish were pretextual based on his protected classes. Regarding claim 1, an individual noted that other GS-9s could not assume the role of backup to the Implant Coordinator due to their workloads, and therefore Complainant was the only employee available to perform the role at the time. The an individual also noted that Complainant did not receive training for the backup responsibilities because he refused to take the training. The Agency reasoned that being the backup to the Implant Coordinator was part of Complainant’s PD when he was hired. Additionally, an individual noted that when a lower-graded employee is assigned to backup a higher-graded position, as here, they are not performing all the duties of the higher-graded position but are just covering the basic functions. With respect to claim 5, an individual noted that additional duties were added to Complainant’s PD because his workload as a Recall Coordinator had diminished, leaving him with very little work for half the day. More specifically, an individual stated that the Recall Coordinator position is typically a collateral duty and most facilities did not have a dedicated Recall Coordinator’s position. In concluding that Complainant did not establish that management’s reasons were pretextual, an individual noted that Complainant provided no documentation, witness testimony, or other evidence in support of his assertion that his race, sexual orientation, or EEO activity were the reasons for the Agency’s actions. Additionally, the Agency determined that Complainant did not show he was subjected to a hostile work environment based on his protected classes, as alleged. 5 As previously noted, the 5-day suspension was later sustained and effective April 24, through April 28, 2017. The record does not reflect whether the proposed 10-day suspension was subsequently implemented by the Agency. While an individual did not specifically address claims 2, 3, and 4, in the analysis portion of its decision, they were included in the factual background section. The matters were also part of the Report of Investigation. Consequently, we find there is sufficient evidence in the record for us to In so finding, an individual noted that Complainant did not establish that the Agency subjected him to unwelcome personal slurs or other denigrating or insulting verbal or physical conduct that was sufficiently severe or pervasive to rise to the level of a hostile work environment. The an individual noted that although an individual alleged he was called homophobic slurs based on his sexual orientation, he provided no evidence, beyond his own assertions, that he was subjected to any such comments.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Supervisory Special Agent (EEO Investigator), GS-1811-14, at the Agency’s Office of EEO Affairs (OEEOA) in Washington, D.C. July 26, 2015, he was therefore “demoted” back to his permanent position of record as a GS-13 Special Agent. Complainant began employment with the Agency on April 22, 1990. His permanent position was as a Special Agent, GS-1811-13, at the Agency’s Washington Field Office. In 2011, Complainant applied for an appointment to one of eight Supervisory Special Agent (SSA) (EEO Investigator, GS-14 positions) in the OEEOA. The position was advertised as a two-year term assignment, with up to three one-year extensions, not to exceed a total of five years. Complainant completed the initial two-year term in July of 2013. He received an extension to July 2014 and another extension to July 2015. During the time at issue, he reported to the Supervisory Attorney Advisor, Chief, Complainants Processing Unit (S1) (Caucasian female). S1 was his immediate supervisor in the Complainants Processing Unit from the time she reported on June 24, 2014. Report of Investigation, (ROI), p. 110. His second level supervisor since 2013 was the Assistant Director, who functioned as the Deputy EEO Officer, Office of Equal Employment Opportunity Affairs, SES (White male) (S2). S1 informed Complainant that she was not recommending him for another extension. The deciding official was S2. Both management officials wanted to increase SSA turnover and improve the functioning of OEEOA. S2 averred that when he assumed his position, OEEOA was largely non-functional and he intended to improve the operations. The average case processing time was 233 days, which was in excess of the 180-day regulatory requirement for EEO investigations. EEO investigators were allocated 45 days of the 180 days to complete their investigations and prepare the reports of investigation. Complainant had been an SSA for four years. S1 affirmed that Complainant’s average case processing time was 84 days. Complainant conceded that he exceeded the 45-day deadline “more times than it was met.” Although S1 told Complainant he was “doing a fine job,” S1 also stated that Complainant failed to communicate with her, and his cases were returned for revisions. Complainant did not receive a third extension and was returned to his GS-13 position of record. Complainant believed that his race was a factor because there is a “perception problem with White male SSAs investigating allegations of discrimination.” He also objected to the Agency’s reliance on “highly subjective criteria” and the Agency’s conflicting reasons for not extending his term. Complainant acknowledged that he was not aware of any Agency policy addressing the renewal or extension of term assignments. ROI, p. 53. Complainant averred, however, that he believed the practice has been to extend each SSA’s term assignment to the maximum of five years. Management has the discretion to extend or terminate a term appointment. There is no guarantee that any employee will be retained for five years. After the completion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s May 21, 2018, motion and issued a summary judgment finding that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the AJ’s decision. The instant appeal followed.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Lead Transportation Security Officer (LTSO), SV-1802, F Band, at the Agency’s Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California. On November 23, 2016, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), sex (female), and color (Dark Brown) when, on February 25, 2016, Complainant was given a One Calendar Day Suspension. On January 5, 2016, Complainant was standing, with three other LTSOs near the briefing area, discussing lane assignments. While Complainant was stating her opinion about the assignments, one of the other officers, who is a Hispanic male coworker, loudly told Complainant to “be quiet.” Complainant then told the male coworker not to talk to her like that – that he could talk to his boyfriend, male friends that way, but not her. Report of Investigation, page 57. The coworker replied “Are you really going to attack my personal life?” One of the other LTSOs pulled Complainant into the breakroom to diffuse the situation. Afterward Complainant averred that she and the coworker “had a discussion and they both apologized.” Later, the Transportation Security Manager (Supervisor 1) requested that Complainant meet with him, the coworker, and the Supervisory Transportation Security Officer (Supervisor 2). The Transportation Security Manager asked for a statement from Complainant and the coworker. Both provided a statement. Complainant averred that she thought that was the end of the matter. On January 13, 2016, the Supervisory Transportation Security Officer (Supervisor 2) brought Complainant into his office and conducted a pre-decisional meeting with the Complainant. He offered the Complainant an opportunity to respond, but he averred the Complainant did not respond. Thereafter, Supervisor 1 issued Complainant a one-day suspension. Supervisor 1 said he suspended her because she confirmed she made the offensive statement and he believed she had a disciplinary history that included a Letter of Reprimand for a similar disrespectful comment toward an officer. He said the Table of Penalties recommended a one-day suspension for circumstances such as Complainant’s conduct and prior offense. Complainant acknowledges that she had received prior counseling, but she maintains that she had not received a prior Letter of Reprimand. She said the coworker was issued a non- disciplinary letter of counseling, although Complainant believes that her comparator received a Letter of Counseling on four occasions preceding this Letter of Counseling. The Agency said that the coworker did not have any discipline for similar conduct in his files at the time of the January 5, 2016 incident. Complainant averred that the race/sex and color discrimination against her is evident because she was given a suspension, but a similarly situated lighter-complexioned male co-worker, who made equally offensive comments and had prior discipline, received only counseling. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation. The Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Over the Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s September 25, 2017 motion for summary judgment. The AJ determined the record was complete and appropriate for the entry of summary judgment because the determinative facts were undisputed. The AJ reasoned that Complainant and the coworker were not similarly situated. The AJ stated that the supervisor suspended Complainant because Complainant told the coworker not to talk to her “like he talked to his boyfriend/boyfriends.” Based on the witness statements, Supervisor 1 understood that the comment referenced the co-worker’s sexual orientation and that the comment was “high in severity and offensive.” The AJ found that Complainant put forth “insufficient evidence to create a genuine dispute of material fact over the description of the incident.” Even if the Complainant meant to refer to the co-worker’s male friendships, the record shows that it “clearly registered with multiple people as a comment about [the co-worker’s] sexual orientation.” The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that the Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. This appeal followed.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Staff Assistant, GS- 14, at the Agency’s VA Office of Construction and Facilities Management (CFM) in Washington, D.C. period of June 2017 to April 25, 2018, she was denied a reasonable accommodation and subjected to a hostile work environment. Specifically, Complainant alleged that: 1. Beginning in June of 2017 and continuing, Complainant’s Program Manager was “badmouthing [Complainant’s] work performance” to her co-workers. 2. During January of 2018, the Program Manager told Complainant that she did not know that Complainant was going on leave, when Complainant had requested leave in October of 2017. 3. On February 21, 2018, the Program Manager denied Complainant’s reasonable accommodation request. 4. During February of 2018, the Program Manager questioned Complainant about her use of the computer system but did not question other employees. 5. In March of 2018, after Complainant requested telework to accommodate her surgery, the Program Manager incorrectly sent Complainant to others, who told Complainant that the approval needed to come from the Program Manager. 6. Despite Complainant’s raising harassment concerns to management, the Associate Executive Director took no action for months to address the alleged harassment. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When, according to the Agency, Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Upon receipt of the Agency’s final decision on the merits, Complainant filed the instant appeal. On appeal, Complainant contends that the Agency improperly issued a Final Agency Decision although Complainant had submitted a timely hearing request. Complainant provided a receipt showing the delivery of her hearing request. She asks that the FAD be reversed and that she be allowed to have a hearing. The record documents that, on or around February 17, 2018, Complainant contacted the Harassment Prevention Program to initiate a sex harassment claim. The Agency acknowledged, in a statement dated February 26, 2019, that Complainant initiated a harassment inquiry. A fact- finding was conducted and concluded that harassment occurred, but Complainant was not told the result of the investigation. See Record (Report of Investigation) at page 361 and 364.

Complainant provided a receipt showing the delivery of her hearing request. She asks that the FAD be reversed and that she be allowed to have a hearing. The record documents that, on or around February 17, 2018, Complainant contacted the Harassment Prevention Program to initiate a sex harassment claim. The an individual acknowledged, in a statement dated February 26, 2019, that Complainant initiated a harassment inquiry. A fact- finding was conducted and concluded that harassment occurred, but Complainant was not told the result of the investigation. See Record (Report of Investigation) at page 361 and 364.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-0592-7 Tax Examining Technician at the Agency’s Small Business/Self-Employed Service Center in Kansas City, Missouri. On October 1, 2017, a Supervisory Tax Examiner became Complainant’s first-line supervisor (S1). At all times relevant to her complaint, a Department Manager was Complainant’s second- line supervisor (S2), and a Program Manager was her third-line supervisor (S3). Complainant is African-American, and her color is light brown. Complainant identified her disability as a speech impediment, stuttering. Complainant averred that she is limited in her ability to speak in front of a crowd, express herself clearly in her meeting, or speak clearly and concisely over the telephone. Complainant alleged that, as a result of her stutter, management believes that she has a learning disability. According to Complainant, she engaged in prior protected activity by filing an EEO complaint in 2015 that named S2 as the responsible management official. Complainant stated that, although S1 was not her supervisor in 2015, S1 was a witness for her EEO complaint. Complainant attended Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) program training in October 2016. Complainant stated that, after she attended the training, she told her former supervisor (FS1) that she was still having a hard time understanding the CSED program. According to Complainant, she met with FS1 to discuss CSED on February 3, 2017. Complainant averred that she became anxious during the discussion, which raised her blood pressure, culminating in Complainant being taken to the hospital to be treated for high blood pressure. According to Complainant, on September 21, 2017, S1 emailed her and stated that she would not receive any more “read time” to learn CSED. Complainant averred that, although S1 was not her supervisor at that time, she had explained to S1 that she was having trouble understanding CSED and that it caused her anxiety. Complainant alleged that S1 told her that she had to get certified on the CSED program because she had been fully trained. According to Complainant, she was not the only employee who had trouble understanding the complexity of the CSED program. Complainant alleged that, as of January 2018, at least eight of her coworkers who attended CSED training were not CSED certified and had not been required to work CSED cases in more than four months. S1 stated that all employees had been trained on CSED and would be required to work the CSED program once they became certified. Complainant stated that she was scheduled to take a vacation day on September 29, 2017. Complainant averred that she told FS1 that she might come in to the office that day and that she would call if she did not come in. According to Complainant, she called FS1 to tell him that she was not coming in and to request leave for the already scheduled vacation day. On September 29, 2017, S1 issued Complainant a memorandum stating that Complainant had not completed her time and attendance for the week because she did not input her leave for September 29, 2017. The memo stated that it was a “courtesy” reminder to Complainant to timely and accurately complete her time and attendance. According to S1, when she became the new supervisor of Complainant’s team, she told the team members that she liked to document conversations in emails and memoranda to have a record of what was discussed. On October 4, 2017, S1 forwarded the team an email with a reminder about the housekeeping guidelines for the office. On October 10, 2017, S1 issued Complainant a memorandum for her failure to follow the housekeeping guidelines. In the memorandum, S1 stated that Complainant used an electric blanket during a training on October 3-4, 2017, and that Complainant did not unplug the blanket when asked by the instructor. S1 averred that electric blankets violated the housekeeping guidelines and asked Complainant to remove her electric blanket from the workplace. According to S1, the reason for the memorandum was that Complainant had ignored the instructor’s request to unplug the blanket, on top of the fact that the electric blanket violated the housekeeping guidelines. According to Complainant, a Caucasian coworker (C1) who had Halloween decorations in her cubicle that violated the guidelines was not issued a memorandum for failing to follow the housekeeping guidelines. Complainant averred that C1 had two 36-inch skeletons on the outside of her cubicle wall that S1 asked her to take down because the decorations violated the fire code. Complainant stated that, when she asked C1 whether she had received anything in writing, C1 told her that she had only received a verbal warning. Complainant stated that, on October 24, 2017, S1 gave her a memorandum documenting an Embedded Quality Review System (EQRS) review, which stated that Complainant’s performance had dropped and that her performance appraisal could be affected. Complainant averred that she asked why the review was in a memorandum and that S1 told her that it was her practice to document such matters in memoranda and that S2 was aware of the matter. Complainant stated that she reached out to the union. According to Complainant, S1 later asked for the memorandum back and tore it up. S1 stated that she asked Complainant for the document back in order to be consistent with other supervisors who did not issue memoranda for performance matters after discussing the issue with S2. According to Complainant, on October 31, 2017, S1 approached her to discuss the suspended cases in her inventory. Complainant stated that she tried to explain how previous supervisors had taught her to work these cases but that S1 interrupted her, talking over her and telling her that she should know better and had been in her position long enough to know how to process cases. Complainant alleged that S1 said, “I’m gonna kill you.” Report of Investigation (ROI) at 121. Complainant stated that she was utterly shocked and amazed by S1’s remark and that she did not feel safe and feared for her life. According to Complainant, S1 also said, “You gonna make me kill you” before she left Complainant’s desk. ROI at 122. Complainant stated that, later on October 31, 2017, S1 emailed her and told her to come to her office. Complainant alleged that, in S1’s office, S1 said, “I could kill you” and gave her negative feedback on her work process. ROI at 122. S1 stated that she was talking to Complainant about her inventory on October 31, 2017. According to S1, she told Complainant to ask the Lead Tax Examining Technician (C2) for help and joked that Complainant could say, “[S1] is going to kill me if I don’t close this case.” ROI at 272. S1 averred that she was joking and stated that both she and Complainant laughed. Complainant denied that S1 was joking when she said she would kill her. According to Complainant, she does not have a friendly relationship with S1, and they do not joke with each other. The record contains an October 31, 2017, email from one of Complainant’s coworkers (C3) to a union representative. In the email, C3 stated that she was at her desk and could hear S1 “going off” on Complainant. ROI at 189. According to C3, Complainant did not understand what S1 was talking about, and S1 was “talking to her like a dog…bullying her.” Id. Complainant averred that she reported S1’s threats to kill her to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA). TIGTA investigated Complainant’s report that S1 threatened to kill her. S1 stated that she was interviewed by TIGTA on November 3, 2017. On November 20, 2017, TIGTA forwarded its report of investigation to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, which declined to prosecute S1 due to lack of federal interest. S1 stated that, as a result of Complainant’s report to TIGTA, she was given a coaching mentor to work on communicating with her subordinates and was required to take training on communication. According to S2, although she had not observed S1 harass Complainant, she knew that S1 struggled with effective communication. S3 stated that S1’s tone can come off as rude and added that S1 has been counseled for unprofessional behavior. Complainant averred that S1 attempted to provide side-by-side instruction on CSED with her on November 15, 2017. Complainant alleged that she was uncomfortable with the situation after S1 had threatened to kill her. Complainant stated that she was nervous and scared to have S1 sitting behind her. According to Complainant, S1 later issued her a memorandum about the instruction, noting that Complainant appeared uncomfortable and distracted and kept pulling her coat and scarf on and off. The record contains a November 15, 2017, memorandum from S1, which discussed the errors Complainant made, noted that Complainant did not ask for help, and added, “You appeared to be distracted, pulling your coat and scarf on and then taking the coat off and turning your desk fan on, while shuffling your notes on your desk.” ROI at 157. Complainant stated that S1 gave her a mid-year evaluation on January 5, 2018. According to Complainant, S1 told her that her performance had declined in several areas and warned, “One more bad review will kill you.” ROI at 136. S1 stated that she told Complainant, “another error is going to kill your accuracy.” ROI at 272. According to S2, the goal was for employees to reach 93 percent customer accuracy, but Complainant’s customer accuracy was 57. percent from October 1, 2017, through February 15, 2018. On December 14, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint, which she subsequently amended, alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), color (light brown), disability (speech impediment), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (prior EEO complaint) when she was subjected to harassment, including when: 1. Since October 1, 2017, management continually issued her memoranda for work performance issues, required her to work a difficult program not required of all employees, threatened to lower her performance evaluation, yelled at her, talked over her, made belittling remarks to her, and made three threatening remarks to the effect of, “I’m going to kill you”; and 2. On January 5, 2018, during her midyear review, S1 stated, “one more bad review will kill you,” and Complainant continued to receive negative memoranda. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted a statement or brief regarding the appeal.

Complainant averred that she is limited in her ability to speak in front of a crowd, express herself clearly in her meeting, or speak clearly and concisely over the telephone. Complainant alleged that, as a result of her stutter, management believes that she has a learning disability. According to Complainant, she engaged in prior protected activity by filing an EEO complaint in 2015 that named S2 as the responsible management official. Complainant stated that, although S1 was not her supervisor in 2015, S1 was a witness for her EEO complaint. Complainant attended Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) program training. Complainant stated that, after she attended the training, she told her former supervisor (FS1) that she was still having a hard time understanding the CSED program. According to Complainant, she met with FS1 to discuss CSED. Complainant averred that she became anxious during the discussion, which raised her blood pressure, culminating in Complainant being taken to the hospital to be treated for high blood pressure. According to Complainant,, S1 emailed her and stated that she would not receive any more “read time” to learn CSED. Complainant averred that, although S1 was not her supervisor at that time, she had explained to S1 that she was having trouble understanding CSED and that it caused her anxiety. Complainant alleged that S1 told her that she had to get certified on the CSED program because she had been fully trained. According to Complainant, she was not the only employee who had trouble understanding the complexity of the CSED program. Complainant alleged that, as of, at least eight of her coworkers who attended CSED training were not CSED certified and had not been required to work CSED cases in more than four months. S1 stated that all employees had been trained on CSED and would be required to work the CSED program once they became certified. Complainant stated that she was scheduled to take a vacation day. Complainant averred that she told FS1 that she might come in to the office that day and that she would call if she did not come in. According to Complainant, she called FS1 to tell him that she was not coming in and to request leave for the already scheduled vacation day., S1 issued Complainant a memorandum stating that Complainant had not completed her time and attendance for the week because she did not input her leave for. The memo stated that it was a “courtesy” reminder to Complainant to timely and accurately complete her time and attendance. According to S1, when she became the new supervisor of Complainant’s team, she told the team members that she liked to document conversations in emails and memoranda to have a record of what was discussed., S1 forwarded the team an email with a reminder about the housekeeping guidelines for the office., S1 issued Complainant a memorandum for her failure to follow the housekeeping guidelines. In the memorandum, S1 stated that Complainant used an electric blanket during a training on October 3-4, 2017, and that Complainant did not unplug the blanket when asked by the instructor. S1 averred that electric blankets violated the housekeeping guidelines and asked Complainant to remove her electric blanket from the workplace. According to S1, the reason for the memorandum was that Complainant had ignored the instructor’s request to unplug the blanket, on top of the fact that the electric blanket violated the housekeeping guidelines. According to Complainant, a Caucasian coworker (C1) who had Halloween decorations in her cubicle that violated the guidelines was not issued a memorandum for failing to follow the housekeeping guidelines. Complainant averred that C1 had two 36-inch skeletons on the outside of her cubicle wall that S1 asked her to take down because the decorations violated the fire code. Complainant stated that, when she asked C1 whether she had received anything in writing, C1 told her that she had only received a verbal warning. Complainant stated that,, S1 gave her a memorandum documenting an Embedded Quality Review System (EQRS) review, which stated that Complainant’s performance had dropped and that her performance appraisal could be affected. Complainant averred that she asked why the review was in a memorandum and that S1 told her that it was her practice to document such matters in memoranda and that S2 was aware of the matter. Complainant stated that she reached out to the union. According to Complainant, S1 later asked for the memorandum back and tore it up. S1 stated that she asked Complainant for the document back in order to be consistent with other supervisors who did not issue memoranda for performance matters after discussing the issue with S2. According to Complainant,, S1 approached her to discuss the suspended cases in her inventory. Complainant stated that she tried to explain how previous supervisors had taught her to work these cases but that S1 interrupted her, talking over her and telling her that she should know better and had been in her position long enough to know how to process cases. Complainant alleged that S1 said, “I’m gonna kill you.” Report of Investigation (ROI) at 121. Complainant stated that she was utterly shocked and amazed by S1’s remark and that she did not feel safe and feared for her life. According to Complainant, S1 also said, “You gonna make me kill you” before she left Complainant’s desk. ROI at 122. Complainant stated that, later, S1 emailed her and told her to come to her office. Complainant alleged that, in S1’s office, S1 said, “I could kill you” and gave her negative feedback on her work process. ROI at 122. S1 stated that she was talking to Complainant about her inventory. According to S1, she told Complainant to ask the Lead Tax Examining Technician (C2) for help and joked that Complainant could say, “[S1] is going to kill me if I don’t close this case.” ROI at 272. S1 averred that she was joking and stated that both she and Complainant laughed. Complainant denied that S1 was joking when she said she would kill her. According to Complainant, she does not have a friendly relationship with S1, and they do not joke with each other. The record contains an, email from one of Complainant’s coworkers (C3) to a union representative. In the email, C3 stated that she was at her desk and could hear S1 “going off” on Complainant. ROI at 189. According to C3, Complainant did not understand what S1 was talking about, and S1 was “talking to her like a dog…bullying her.” Id. Complainant averred that she reported S1’s threats to kill her to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA). TIGTA investigated Complainant’s report that S1 threatened to kill her. S1 stated that she was interviewed by TIGTA., TIGTA forwarded its report of investigation to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, which declined to prosecute S1 due to lack of federal interest. S1 stated that, as a result of Complainant’s report to TIGTA, she was given a coaching mentor to work on communicating with her subordinates and was required to take training on communication. According to S2, although she had not observed S1 harass Complainant, she knew that S1 struggled with effective communication. S3 stated that S1’s tone can come off as rude and added that S1 has been counseled for unprofessional behavior. Complainant averred that S1 attempted to provide side-by-side instruction on CSED with her. Complainant alleged that she was uncomfortable with the situation after S1 had threatened to kill her. Complainant stated that she was nervous and scared to have S1 sitting behind her. According to Complainant, S1 later issued her a memorandum about the instruction, noting that Complainant appeared uncomfortable and distracted and kept pulling her coat and scarf on and off. The record contains a, memorandum from S1, which discussed the errors Complainant made, noted that Complainant did not ask for help, and added, “You appeared to be distracted, pulling your coat and scarf on and then taking the coat off and turning your desk fan on, while shuffling your notes on your desk.” ROI at 157. Complainant stated that S1 gave her a mid-year evaluation. According to Complainant, S1 told her that her performance had declined in several areas and warned, “One more bad review will kill you.” ROI at 136. S1 stated that she told Complainant, “another error is going to kill your accuracy.” ROI at 272. According to S2, the goal was for employees to reach 93 percent customer accuracy, but Complainant’s customer accuracy was 57. percent, through., Complainant filed an EEO complaint, which she subsequently amended, alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), color (light brown), disability (speech impediment), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (prior EEO complaint) when she was subjected to harassment, including when: 1., management continually issued her memoranda for work performance issues, required her to work a difficult program not required of all employees, threatened to lower her performance evaluation, yelled at her, talked over her, made belittling remarks to her, and made three threatening remarks to the effect of, “I’m going to kill you”; and 2., during her midyear review, S1 stated, “one more bad review will kill you,” and Complainant continued to receive negative memoranda. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted a statement or brief regarding the appeal.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Staff Assistant, GS- 14, at the Agency’s VA Office of Construction and Facilities Management (CFM) in Washington, D.C. period of June 2017 to April 25, 2018, she was denied a reasonable accommodation and subjected to a hostile work environment. Specifically, Complainant alleged that: 1. Beginning in June of 2017 and continuing, Complainant’s Program Manager was “badmouthing [Complainant’s] work performance” to her co-workers. 2. During January of 2018, the Program Manager told Complainant that she did not know that Complainant was going on leave, when Complainant had requested leave in October of 2017. 3. On February 21, 2018, the Program Manager denied Complainant’s reasonable accommodation request. 4. During February of 2018, the Program Manager questioned Complainant about her use of the computer system but did not question other employees. 5. In March of 2018, after Complainant requested telework to accommodate her surgery, the Program Manager incorrectly sent Complainant to others, who told Complainant that the approval needed to come from the Program Manager. 6. Despite Complainant’s raising harassment concerns to management, the Associate Executive Director took no action for months to address the alleged harassment. 2 At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When, according to the Agency, Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. Upon receipt of the Agency’s final decision on the merits, Complainant filed the instant appeal. On appeal, Complainant contends that the Agency improperly issued a Final Agency Decision although Complainant had submitted a timely hearing request. Complainant provided a receipt showing the delivery of her hearing request. She asks that the FAD be reversed and that she be allowed to have a hearing. The record documents that, on or around February 17, 2018, Complainant contacted the Harassment Prevention Program to initiate a sex harassment claim. The Agency acknowledged, in a statement dated February 26, 2019, that Complainant initiated a harassment inquiry. A fact- finding was conducted and concluded that harassment occurred, but Complainant was not told the result of the investigation. See Record (Report of Investigation) at page 361 and 364.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-0592-7 Tax Examining Technician at the Agency’s Small Business/Self-Employed Service Center in Kansas City, Missouri. On October 1, 2017, a Supervisory Tax Examiner became Complainant’s first-line supervisor (S1). At all times relevant to her complaint, a Department Manager was Complainant’s second- line supervisor (S2), and a Program Manager was her third-line supervisor (S3). Complainant is African-American, and her color is light brown. Complainant identified her disability as a speech impediment, stuttering. Complainant averred that she is limited in her ability to speak in front of a crowd, express herself clearly in her meeting, or speak clearly and concisely over the telephone. Complainant alleged that, as a result of her stutter, management believes that she has a learning disability. According to Complainant, she engaged in prior protected activity by filing an EEO complaint in 2015 that named S2 as the responsible management official. Complainant stated that, although S1 was not her supervisor in 2015, S1 was a witness for her EEO complaint. Complainant attended Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) program training in October 2016. Complainant stated that, after she attended the training, she told her former supervisor (FS1) that she was still having a hard time understanding the CSED program. According to Complainant, she met with FS1 to discuss CSED on February 3, 2017. Complainant averred that she became anxious during the discussion, which raised her blood pressure, culminating in Complainant being taken to the hospital to be treated for high blood pressure. According to Complainant, on September 21, 2017, S1 emailed her and stated that she would not receive any more “read time” to learn CSED. Complainant averred that, although S1 was not her supervisor at that time, she had explained to S1 that she was having trouble understanding CSED and that it caused her anxiety. Complainant alleged that S1 told her that she had to get certified on the CSED program because she had been fully trained. According to Complainant, she was not the only employee who had trouble understanding the complexity of the CSED program. Complainant alleged that, as of January 2018, at least eight of her coworkers who attended CSED training were not CSED certified and had not been required to work CSED cases in more than four months. S1 stated that all employees had been trained on CSED and would be required to work the CSED program once they became certified. Complainant stated that she was scheduled to take a vacation day on September 29, 2017. Complainant averred that she told FS1 that she might come in to the office that day and that she would call if she did not come in. According to Complainant, she called FS1 to tell him that she was not coming in and to request leave for the already scheduled vacation day. On September 29, 2017, S1 issued Complainant a memorandum stating that Complainant had not completed her time and attendance for the week because she did not input her leave for September 29, 2017. The memo stated that it was a “courtesy” reminder to Complainant to timely and accurately complete her time and attendance. According to S1, when she became the new supervisor of Complainant’s team, she told the team members that she liked to document conversations in emails and memoranda to have a record of what was discussed. On October 4, 2017, S1 forwarded the team an email with a reminder about the housekeeping guidelines for the office. On October 10, 2017, S1 issued Complainant a memorandum for her failure to follow the housekeeping guidelines. In the memorandum, S1 stated that Complainant used an electric blanket during a training on October 3-4, 2017, and that Complainant did not unplug the blanket when asked by the instructor. S1 averred that electric blankets violated the housekeeping guidelines and asked Complainant to remove her electric blanket from the workplace. According to S1, the reason for the memorandum was that Complainant had ignored the instructor’s request to unplug the blanket, on top of the fact that the electric blanket violated the housekeeping guidelines. According to Complainant, a Caucasian coworker (C1) who had Halloween decorations in her cubicle that violated the guidelines was not issued a memorandum for failing to follow the housekeeping guidelines. Complainant averred that C1 had two 36-inch skeletons on the outside of her cubicle wall that S1 asked her to take down because the decorations violated the fire code. Complainant stated that, when she asked C1 whether she had received anything in writing, C1 told her that she had only received a verbal warning. Complainant stated that, on October 24, 2017, S1 gave her a memorandum documenting an Embedded Quality Review System (EQRS) review, which stated that Complainant’s performance had dropped and that her performance appraisal could be affected. Complainant averred that she asked why the review was in a memorandum and that S1 told her that it was her practice to document such matters in memoranda and that S2 was aware of the matter. Complainant stated that she reached out to the union. According to Complainant, S1 later asked for the memorandum back and tore it up. S1 stated that she asked Complainant for the document back in order to be consistent with other supervisors who did not issue memoranda for performance matters after discussing the issue with S2. According to Complainant, on October 31, 2017, S1 approached her to discuss the suspended cases in her inventory. Complainant stated that she tried to explain how previous supervisors had taught her to work these cases but that S1 interrupted her, talking over her and telling her that she should know better and had been in her position long enough to know how to process cases. Complainant alleged that S1 said, “I’m gonna kill you.” Report of Investigation (ROI) at 121. Complainant stated that she was utterly shocked and amazed by S1’s remark and that she did not feel safe and feared for her life. According to Complainant, S1 also said, “You gonna make me kill you” before she left Complainant’s desk. ROI at 122. Complainant stated that, later on October 31, 2017, S1 emailed her and told her to come to her office. Complainant alleged that, in S1’s office, S1 said, “I could kill you” and gave her negative feedback on her work process. ROI at 122. S1 stated that she was talking to Complainant about her inventory on October 31, 2017. According to S1, she told Complainant to ask the Lead Tax Examining Technician (C2) for help and joked that Complainant could say, “[S1] is going to kill me if I don’t close this case.” ROI at 272. S1 averred that she was joking and stated that both she and Complainant laughed. Complainant denied that S1 was joking when she said she would kill her. According to Complainant, she does not have a friendly relationship with S1, and they do not joke with each other. The record contains an October 31, 2017, email from one of Complainant’s coworkers (C3) to a union representative. In the email, C3 stated that she was at her desk and could hear S1 “going off” on Complainant. ROI at 189. According to C3, Complainant did not understand what S1 was talking about, and S1 was “talking to her like a dog…bullying her.” Id. Complainant averred that she reported S1’s threats to kill her to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA). TIGTA investigated Complainant’s report that S1 threatened to kill her. S1 stated that she was interviewed by TIGTA on November 3, 2017. On November 20, 2017, TIGTA forwarded its report of investigation to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, which declined to prosecute S1 due to lack of federal interest. S1 stated that, as a result of Complainant’s report to TIGTA, she was given a coaching mentor to work on communicating with her subordinates and was required to take training on communication. According to S2, although she had not observed S1 harass Complainant, she knew that S1 struggled with effective communication. S3 stated that S1’s tone can come off as rude and added that S1 has been counseled for unprofessional behavior. Complainant averred that S1 attempted to provide side-by-side instruction on CSED with her on November 15, 2017. Complainant alleged that she was uncomfortable with the situation after S1 had threatened to kill her. Complainant stated that she was nervous and scared to have S1 sitting behind her. According to Complainant, S1 later issued her a memorandum about the instruction, noting that Complainant appeared uncomfortable and distracted and kept pulling her coat and scarf on and off. The record contains a November 15, 2017, memorandum from S1, which discussed the errors Complainant made, noted that Complainant did not ask for help, and added, “You appeared to be distracted, pulling your coat and scarf on and then taking the coat off and turning your desk fan on, while shuffling your notes on your desk.” ROI at 157. Complainant stated that S1 gave her a mid-year evaluation on January 5, 2018. According to Complainant, S1 told her that her performance had declined in several areas and warned, “One more bad review will kill you.” ROI at 136. S1 stated that she told Complainant, “another error is going to kill your accuracy.” ROI at 272. According to S2, the goal was for employees to reach 93 percent customer accuracy, but Complainant’s customer accuracy was 57. percent from October 1, 2017, through February 15, 2018. On December 14, 2017, Complainant filed an EEO complaint, which she subsequently amended, alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American), color (light brown), disability (speech impediment), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (prior EEO complaint) when she was subjected to harassment, including when: 1. Since October 1, 2017, management continually issued her memoranda for work performance issues, required her to work a difficult program not required of all employees, threatened to lower her performance evaluation, yelled at her, talked over her, made belittling remarks to her, and made three threatening remarks to the effect of, “I’m going to kill you”; and 2. On January 5, 2018, during her midyear review, S1 stated, “one more bad review will kill you,” and Complainant continued to receive negative memoranda. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. Neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted a statement or brief regarding the appeal.
